title: Seasons: why a leaning Earth has summer and winter at the same moment

summary.text: The Earth is nearest to the Sun in early January, when Delhi is at its coldest. So what really makes the seasons? In this lesson you will test lean against distance with a torch, carry a leaning ball round a lamp for one whole year, and compare the day lengths of four Indian cities. You will also find out why Pongal comes three weeks after the shortest day, and why different peoples count two, four, six or twenty-four seasons.
summary.art: A leaning ball on a steel tumbler beside a small lamp on a dark floor, with one half of the ball lit, and a child kneeling to count pen dots along a rubber band on the ball.

intro.hook: On about 3 January the Earth is 5 million kilometres nearer to the Sun than on about 4 July. Yet January is the coldest month in Delhi and Srinagar. And on that same January day, children in Sydney are swimming in the sea in full summer. How can one Earth, under one Sun, be in winter and in summer at the same moment?
intro.text: Many grown-ups say that summer comes when the Earth is close to the Sun. It is a sensible guess, because a fire feels hotter when you step nearer. In this lesson you test that guess yourself. You measure how much a patch of torchlight changes when the torch moves away, and how much it changes when the ground leans. Then you carry a leaning ball round a lamp and count the hours of daylight. The answer you find explains the solstices, the monsoon, zero shadow day in Chennai and the date of Pongal.
intro.art: A split picture of the same January day: on the left a child in a sweater in a foggy Delhi lane, on the right a child in a sun hat on a bright Sydney beach, with one small Sun drawn between them.

outcomes: By the end I can tell rotation from revolution, and say how long each takes and what each gives us.
By the end I can use my torch results to show that the slant of sunlight changes the heating far more than the Earth's distance from the Sun does.
By the end I can use a leaning ball to explain why the two halves of the Earth have opposite seasons, and why the axis must keep pointing the same way.
By the end I can name the two solstices and the two equinoxes, give their dates, and say where the noon Sun is overhead on each.
By the end I can explain why day length changes little in Kanyakumari, more in Delhi and most near the poles.
By the end I can explain how the seasons drive the monsoon winds, and why the hottest days come after the longest day.
By the end I can compare different ways of counting seasons, in India and elsewhere, and say what each count is watching.
By the end I can explain why Pongal and Makar Sankranti now come about three weeks after the December solstice.

terms.meaning: The spinning of the Earth round its own axis. One rotation takes about 24 hours and gives us day and night.
terms.example: A spinning pambaram, the wooden top, rotates round its nail.
terms.art: A wooden top spinning on a floor, with a curved arrow round it.

terms.meaning: The journey of the Earth round the Sun. One revolution takes one year, about 365 days and 6 hours.
terms.example: A child running once round a lamp post has made one revolution round it.
terms.art: A small Earth on a dotted circle round the Sun, with an arrow showing one full trip.

terms.meaning: The path that one body follows round another. The Earth's orbit round the Sun is almost a circle.
terms.example: The Moon has an orbit round the Earth, and the Earth has an orbit round the Sun.
terms.art: The Sun in the middle with a thin, nearly round path drawn round it and a small Earth on the path.

terms.meaning: The line through the North Pole and the South Pole that the Earth spins round. Nobody can see it. It is a line we imagine.
terms.example: The nail of a spinning top lies along the top's axis.
terms.art: A ball with a thin line through it from top to bottom, labelled North Pole and South Pole.

terms.meaning: The lean of the Earth's axis. The axis leans about 23 and a half degrees away from standing straight up on the orbit.
terms.example: A ball leaning about a quarter of the way from standing up to lying flat has roughly the Earth's tilt.
terms.art: Two balls with axis lines: one standing straight up, one leaning, with the angle between them marked 23.5 degrees.

terms.meaning: A stretched circle, like the top of a tumbler seen from the side. The Earth's orbit is an ellipse that is stretched very little.
terms.example: A round torch patch becomes an ellipse when the wall leans.
terms.art: A circle and a slightly stretched oval drawn side by side.

terms.meaning: The point on the orbit where the Earth is nearest to the Sun. The Earth is there in early January.
terms.example: At perihelion the Sun is about 147 million kilometres away.
terms.art: The Earth on its orbit at the point nearest the Sun, with a short arrow between them marked January.

terms.meaning: The point on the orbit where the Earth is farthest from the Sun. The Earth is there in early July.
terms.example: At aphelion the Sun is about 152 million kilometres away.
terms.art: The Earth on its orbit at the point farthest from the Sun, with a longer arrow marked July.

terms.meaning: Half of the Earth. The equator divides the Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.
terms.example: India is in the Northern Hemisphere. Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere.
terms.art: A globe with the top half shaded one colour and the bottom half another, and India and Australia marked.

terms.meaning: One of the two days in the year when the noon Sun is as far north or as far south as it ever goes. One is about 21 June and the other about 21 December.
terms.example: About 21 June is the longest day of the year everywhere in India.
terms.art: The Earth at two opposite points of its orbit, once with the north leaning to the Sun and once leaning away.

terms.meaning: One of the two days in the year when the noon Sun is overhead at the equator. Day and night are then nearly equal everywhere. They fall about 20 March and 23 September.
terms.example: On the March equinox, Chennai and Srinagar both get about 12 hours of daylight.
terms.art: The Earth side-on to the Sun, with the line between day and night passing through both poles.

terms.meaning: The line round the Earth, 23 and a half degrees north of the equator, where the noon Sun is overhead on the June solstice.
terms.example: The Tropic of Cancer crosses eight Indian states, from Gujarat to Mizoram.
terms.art: A map of India with a dotted line across its middle, passing through Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal.

terms.meaning: The line round the Earth, 23 and a half degrees south of the equator, where the noon Sun is overhead on the December solstice.
terms.example: The Tropic of Capricorn crosses Australia, southern Africa and South America.
terms.art: A world map with two dotted lines, one above and one below the equator.

terms.meaning: The line round the Earth, about 66 and a half degrees north. North of it the Sun stays up all night on at least one day in June, and stays down all day on at least one day in December.
terms.example: In Tromso in Norway, the Sun does not set for about two months in summer.
terms.art: A view down on the top of the globe with a dashed circle round the North Pole and a low Sun shining across it.

terms.meaning: A day when the noon Sun is exactly overhead, so an upright pole has no shadow at noon. It happens twice a year, and only in places between the two tropics.
terms.example: Chennai and Bengaluru have zero shadow days about 24 April and 18 August.
terms.art: A steel tumbler standing in bright noon sunlight on a terrace floor with no shadow round it.

terms.meaning: The two halves of the Sun's yearly swing. In Uttarayana the noon Sun moves north, from the December solstice to the June solstice. In Dakshinayana it moves south again.
terms.example: During Uttarayana the days in India grow longer week by week.
terms.art: A horizon with the noon Sun shown at three heights, and arrows going up on one side and down on the other.

terms.meaning: A season in the old Indian count, which divides the year into six ritus of about two months each.
terms.example: Varsha ritu is the season of the rains.
terms.art: A wheel cut into six equal parts, each with a small drawing: a flower, a hot Sun, a rain cloud, a clear Moon, mist and dew.

terms.meaning: A wind that blows from one direction for part of the year and from the opposite direction for another part, bringing a wet season and a dry season.
terms.example: The south-west monsoon reaches Kerala about 1 June. The north-east monsoon brings Chennai's rain in October to December.
terms.art: A map of India with thick arrows from the south-west sea onto the land in one colour, and arrows from the north-east in another.

terms.meaning: The very slow wobble of the Earth's axis. The axis traces one full circle in about 26,000 years, the way a leaning top slowly circles.
terms.example: Because of precession, Makar Sankranti has slipped about three weeks away from the December solstice.
terms.art: A leaning spinning top with a dotted circle traced in the air by the top end of its axis.

terms.meaning: A year with one extra day, 29 February. It keeps the calendar in step with the seasons, because one revolution takes about a quarter of a day more than 365 days.
terms.example: 2024 and 2028 are leap years.
terms.art: A calendar page for February with the box for the 29th drawn in a bright colour.

explanations.concept: Two motions at once: rotation and revolution
explanations.definition: The Earth rotates on its axis once in about 24 hours, which gives day and night. At the same time it revolves round the Sun once in about 365 days and 6 hours, which gives the year.
explanations.description: The Earth does both things together, like a spinning top that is also sliding round a table. The spin carries you from day into night and back. The journey round the Sun is far longer. The orbit is about 940 million kilometres long, and the Earth covers about 30 kilometres of it every second. We feel nothing, because the ground, the air and our bodies all move together at a steady speed. The extra 6 hours each year add up to one whole day in four years. That is why a leap year gets a 29th of February.
examples: A day is one rotation. A year is one revolution.
In the time you take to say 'Kanyakumari', the Earth has moved about 30 kilometres along its orbit.
Your age in years is the number of times you have gone round the Sun.

perspectives.who: Panchangam makers and ships' navigators
perspectives.explanation: They work as if the Earth stood still and the Sun travelled through the twelve rashis in a year. This picture matches what our eyes see, and it gives the right dates for sunrise, sankrantis and eclipses. For finding your way at sea it is the easier picture to use.

perspectives.who: Aryabhata in 499 CE and Nicolaus Copernicus in 1543
perspectives.explanation: Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins, and that the stars only seem to move, as the bank seems to move to a person in a boat. Copernicus added that the Earth also goes round the Sun. Later evidence supported this. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured a nearby star shifting back and forth each year, as it should if we are the ones moving.

perspectives.who: Physicists since Isaac Newton and Albert Einstein
perspectives.explanation: The Earth and the Sun both go round their shared balance point, which lies deep inside the Sun because the Sun is so heavy. You may describe the motion from any place you like. The Sun-centred picture is chosen because it makes the rules of motion simplest.

explanations.art: A small Earth with a curved arrow round itself labelled 24 hours, travelling on a large dotted circle round the Sun labelled 1 year.
explanations.context: This card sorts out the Earth's two motions, because the seasons need both of them.

explanations.concept: The orbit is almost a circle, and the Earth is nearest the Sun in January
explanations.definition: The Earth's orbit is an ellipse that is stretched so little that it looks like a circle. The Earth is nearest the Sun, at perihelion, in early January, and farthest, at aphelion, in early July.
explanations.description: In The True Shape of the Year you drew the orbit to scale. On a circle 20 centimetres wide, the Sun sits less than 2 millimetres from the centre. The nearest distance is about 147 million kilometres and the farthest about 152 million kilometres. That is a difference of about 3 parts in every 100. Books often draw the orbit as a long oval because they show it tilted, as if seen from the side. The drawing is honest about the view, but it leaves a wrong picture in the mind. The Earth also moves a little faster when it is nearer the Sun. So the half of the year from the September equinox to the March equinox is about 179 days long, and the other half is about 186 days.
examples: Early January: about 147 million kilometres from the Sun.
Early July: about 152 million kilometres from the Sun.
A steel plate seen from the side looks like a long oval, though it is round.
explanations.art: A view from above of a nearly perfect circle with the Sun a tiny step off the centre, the nearest point marked January and the farthest marked July.
explanations.context: This card gives the real shape of the Earth's path and the real dates of nearest and farthest. They are the facts that the distance idea of seasons has to face.
explanations.one_view: The distances are measured by radar and by spacecraft to within a few metres, and no scientist disputes the dates of nearest and farthest.

explanations.definition: Sunlight that arrives at a slant is spread over more ground, so each patch of ground gets less of it. This slant changes through the year far more than the Earth's distance from the Sun does.
explanations.description: In Lean or Distance, moving the torch 1 centimetre further in 30 made the patch only a hair wider. Leaning the card as Delhi leans in December made the patch more than one and a half times as long. The same light was spread over much more card, so each square centimetre got much less. In Delhi the noon Sun is about 5 degrees from overhead in June and about 52 degrees from overhead in December. So each square metre of Delhi ground gets only about 6 parts in 10 of the noon sunlight in December that it gets in June. In Chennai the swing is smaller, from about 10 degrees to about 37 degrees, so Chennai's winter is mild. Summer also has longer days, so the ground is heated for more hours. The two effects, steeper light and longer days, work together.
examples: A dosa batter poured on a tilted tawa spreads into a long thin oval.
Morning and evening sunlight is gentle because it comes at a low slant.
Solar panels are tilted to face the Sun squarely.

perspectives.who: Milutin Milankovitch, a Serbian scientist of the 1920s, and climate scientists after him
perspectives.explanation: Distance is small but not nothing. In early January the whole Earth gets about 7 parts in 100 more sunlight than in early July. This falls on the southern summer, where wide oceans soak it up. Over tens of thousands of years, slow changes in the orbit and the tilt help to start and end ice ages.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the air
perspectives.explanation: Slant does a second thing. Low sunlight passes through much more air before it reaches the ground. When the Sun is 30 degrees above the horizon, its light crosses twice as much air as when it is overhead. More of it is scattered and soaked up on the way.

explanations.art: Two equal beams of sunlight: one hitting the ground straight and lighting a small bright patch, the other hitting at a slant and lighting a long pale patch.
explanations.context: This card explains the result of Lean or Distance. It is the heart of why seasons happen.

explanations.concept: The axis leans, and keeps pointing the same way
explanations.definition: The Earth's axis leans about 23 and a half degrees from upright on its orbit. All year the axis keeps pointing to the same far place in space, close to the Pole Star.
explanations.description: In The Leaning Ball, the top dot of the ball pointed at the same wall at every place round the lamp. That is the key. In June the northern end of the axis leans towards the Sun. Six months later the Earth is on the other side of the Sun. The axis has not turned, so now the northern end leans away. A spinning body keeps its axis steady, as a fast top stays up and a slow top falls over. The northern end of the axis points almost at the Pole Star, called Dhruva in India. That is why Dhruva stays in one place in the sky while other stars circle round.
examples: A spinning top keeps its lean while it slides across the floor.
The Pole Star is always in the north, at every hour and in every season.
With the ball standing upright, every place on it got the same light all year.

perspectives.who: Physicists who study spinning things
perspectives.explanation: A spinning body keeps the direction of its axis unless something twists it. Over one year the twist on the Earth is far too small to notice. So for a lifetime, the axis is as good as fixed.

perspectives.who: Hipparchus, about 127 BCE, and astronomers of slow time
perspectives.explanation: The axis is not fixed for ever. The pull of the Moon and the Sun on the Earth's bulging middle makes the axis wobble in a slow circle, once in about 26,000 years. This is precession. In about 12,000 years the bright star Vega, called Abhijit, will be near the north point of the sky, and Dhruva will circle like any other star.

explanations.art: The Sun in the middle and the Earth drawn at four points of its orbit, with the axis leaning the same way, towards the right, in all four.
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in The Leaning Ball: one steady lean gives opposite seasons on opposite sides of the Sun.

explanations.concept: Four marker days: two solstices and two equinoxes
explanations.definition: A solstice is a day when the noon Sun is as far north or south as it goes. An equinox is a day when the noon Sun is overhead at the equator. They fall about 21 June, 23 September, 21 December and 20 March.
explanations.description: About 21 June the noon Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, which crosses India from Gujarat to Mizoram. This is the longest day in India. About 21 December the noon Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, and India has its shortest day. On the two equinoxes the Sun is overhead at the equator, and the line between day and night passes through both poles. Between the tropics, the overhead Sun passes every place twice a year. Those are the zero shadow days. Chennai and Bengaluru have them about 24 April and 18 August, Mumbai about 15 May and 27 July, and Kanyakumari about 10 April and 1 September. Delhi, Lucknow and Srinagar lie north of the Tropic of Cancer, so the Sun is never overhead there. In June the noon Sun in Chennai is a little to the north, so noon shadows point south.
examples: 21 June: longest day in India, shortest day in Australia.
The word solstice means 'the Sun stands still', because the noon Sun stops moving north or south for a few days.
Nowruz, the new year of Iran and of the Parsis, is on the March equinox.

perspectives.who: Astronomers
perspectives.explanation: Each season begins on a solstice or an equinox. By this count, northern summer starts about 21 June and winter about 21 December.

perspectives.who: Weather offices in many countries
perspectives.explanation: Seasons should follow the weather and be easy to count. So summer is the three hottest whole months, and each season begins on the first day of a month.

perspectives.who: The old Chinese and old Irish calendars
perspectives.explanation: The solstice is the middle of the season, not its start. The longest day is called midsummer. In the Chinese calendar summer begins about 5 May, when the light is growing strong, and ends in early August.

explanations.art: The Earth at four points of its orbit labelled 21 June, 23 September, 21 December and 20 March, with a small arrow showing where the noon Sun is overhead at each.
explanations.context: This card names the four days that mark the Earth's place on its orbit. Calendars and festivals all over the world are built on them.

explanations.concept: Day length: a small change at Kanyakumari, a large one at Delhi, six months at the poles
explanations.definition: Because the axis leans, the share of each day that a place spends in sunlight changes through the year. The change is zero at the equator and grows towards the poles.
explanations.description: In Four Cities, Two Days, the day in Kanyakumari was less than one hour longer in June than in December. In Chennai the difference was about one and a half hours, in Delhi about three and a half, and in Srinagar about four and a half. In The Leaning Ball you saw why. A ring near the leaning pole has most of its circle in the light in summer. A ring near the equator is always cut nearly in half. North of the Arctic Circle the Sun does not set at all for part of the summer. At the North Pole there is one long day of about six months and one long night of about six months. At the equator, every day of the year is close to 12 hours long.
examples: Kanyakumari: about 12 hours 36 minutes on 21 June and 11 hours 39 minutes on 21 December.
Delhi: about 13 hours 59 minutes on 21 June and 10 hours 20 minutes on 21 December.
In Tromso in Norway the Sun stays up all night from about 20 May to 22 July.
At the North Pole the Sun stays low in the sky, so its rays arrive at a slant. The ground stays cold, even on the long summer day.

perspectives.who: A person who draws the Earth and the Sun with straight rays
perspectives.explanation: On an equinox, exactly half of every ring is lit. So day and night are exactly 12 hours each, everywhere.

perspectives.who: A person who watches real sunrises
perspectives.explanation: The air bends sunlight, so we see the Sun a few minutes before it has truly cleared the horizon. The Sun is also a wide disc, not a point. So on the equinox the day is about 12 hours and 7 minutes long. Day and night are truly equal a few days before the March equinox.

explanations.art: A leaning globe with one half lit, and three rings drawn round it at different heights, each showing how much of the ring is in the light.
explanations.context: This card explains why days grow and shrink through the year, and why they change more in the north of India than in the south.

explanations.concept: Opposite seasons in the two hemispheres, and a different year near the equator
explanations.definition: When the northern end of the axis leans towards the Sun, the Northern Hemisphere has summer and the Southern Hemisphere has winter. Six months later it is the other way round.
explanations.description: In The Leaning Ball the northern ring had the most lit dots at the very place where the southern ring had the fewest. So Christmas in Australia, Argentina and South Africa comes in high summer, and schools there take their long summer holiday in December and January. Near the equator the year has another shape. In Singapore, or at the southern tip of India, the Sun passes overhead twice a year and day length hardly changes. People there notice wet months and dry months more than hot and cold ones. Kerala and coastal Tamil Nadu stay warm all year, and their seasons are counted by the rains.
examples: When it is winter in Srinagar it is summer in Sydney.
In June, penguins in Antarctica stand through weeks of night while Arctic terns in the far north have daylight all night.
Kochi's hottest month and its coolest month differ by only about 3 degrees Celsius.
explanations.art: A leaning Earth with the Sun's rays coming from the left: the top half labelled summer and the bottom half winter, with a small picture of India above and Australia below.
explanations.context: This card follows the leaning ball to the other half of the world, and to the places near the equator where 'summer and winter' hardly fit.
explanations.one_view: This follows straight from the lean of the axis, and weather records from both hemispheres match it every year.

explanations.concept: The hottest days come after the longest day
explanations.definition: The ground, the sea and the air take weeks to warm up and weeks to cool down. So the hottest part of the year comes some weeks after the June solstice, and the coldest some weeks after the December solstice. This delay is called seasonal lag.
explanations.description: The same thing happens every day. The Sun is highest at noon, but the hottest hour is usually about 2 or 3 in the afternoon. The ground is still gaining more heat than it loses. Over the year, Delhi's shortest day is about 21 December, but its coldest weeks are in January. The sea warms and cools more slowly than the land, so places by the sea lag more. In much of the world the hottest month is July or August. India is different for a reason of its own. The monsoon clouds arrive in June and shade the land. So the hottest weeks in most of India are in May. In Tamil Nadu the hottest stretch of May is called Agni Nakshatram or Kathiri Veyil.
examples: A tawa stays hot for a while after the burner is turned off.
The hottest hour of the day is in the afternoon, not at noon.
Delhi is coldest in January, weeks after the shortest day.
explanations.art: A graph with two wavy lines over a year: one for hours of daylight peaking in June, and one for temperature peaking a few weeks later.
explanations.context: This card explains a puzzle in the dates: why the hottest and coldest weeks do not fall on the solstices.
explanations.one_view: Seasonal lag is measured at every weather station on Earth. Scientists differ only about its exact size from place to place.

explanations.definition: A monsoon is a wind that changes direction with the seasons. In India the south-west monsoon blows from the sea from June to September, and the north-east monsoon blows from the land and the Bay of Bengal from October to December.
explanations.description: As the noon Sun moves north in April and May, the land of India heats strongly. Moist winds from the Indian Ocean then blow onto the land and bring rain. The south-west monsoon reaches Kerala about 1 June and covers the whole country by about 8 July. From mid-September it draws back. Then the winds turn. The north-east monsoon brings Tamil Nadu about half of its rain for the year. Everyone agrees that the tilt of the Earth sets this yearly rhythm. Scientists still argue about exactly how the heating makes the rain.
examples: Onam in Kerala comes in August or September, when the heaviest south-west rains are over and the first rice is harvested.
Chennai gets most of its rain in October to December, when much of India is dry.
The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word mausim, which means season.

perspectives.who: Edmond Halley, an English astronomer, in 1686
perspectives.explanation: The monsoon is a giant sea breeze. Land heats faster than sea, so in summer the air over the hot land rises and moist sea air rushes in to take its place. In winter the land is cooler than the sea, and the wind turns round.

perspectives.who: Sulochana Gadgil of the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, with D. R. Sikka in 1980
perspectives.explanation: The monsoon is a belt of rain clouds round the Earth that follows the overhead Sun north in summer and south in winter. India's monsoon is that belt arriving over the land. This explains why the rain comes in bursts and breaks, and why the hottest land is often not the wettest.

perspectives.who: William Boos and Zhiming Kuang in 2010
perspectives.explanation: The Himalaya matter most as a wall. The mountains stop cold, dry air from Central Asia mixing with the warm, moist air over India. In computer models the monsoon stays strong even when the high Tibetan Plateau is taken away, as long as the wall of mountains stays.

explanations.art: Two small maps of India side by side: in the first, arrows sweep in from the south-west sea in June, and in the second, arrows come from the north-east in November.
explanations.context: This card connects the tilt of the Earth to the rains that India lives by, and shows that the link is still being worked out.

explanations.definition: A season is a part of the year that people mark off because the sky, the weather or living beings change. The Earth's orbit gives four marker days. How many seasons to count, and where each one starts, is a choice that different peoples have made in different ways.
explanations.description: The six ritus of the Sanskrit calendar are Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira. The old Tamil grammar, the Tolkappiyam, also counts six, with other names and starting points: Kaar, Koothir, Munpani, Pinpani, Ilavenil and Mudhuvenil. India's weather office counts four. Each count fits the land where it was made and the things its makers needed to know. None of them is the one true count.
examples: Varsha, the season of rains, has no partner in the four-season count of Europe.
Munpani and Pinpani are the Tamil seasons of early dew and late dew.
A child in Kochi and a child in Shimla may need different season calendars.

perspectives.who: The Sanskrit and Tamil traditions of India
perspectives.explanation: Six seasons of two months each. The rains and the dew seasons get their own names, because farming depends on them. The Tamil count begins the cycle with Kaar, the rains.

perspectives.who: The India Meteorological Department
perspectives.explanation: Four seasons, set by the winds and the rain: winter in January and February, the hot weather from March to May, the south-west monsoon from June to September, and the post-monsoon from October to December.

perspectives.who: The Noongar people of south-western Australia
perspectives.explanation: Six seasons with no fixed dates: Birak, Bunuru, Djeran, Makuru, Djilba and Kambarang. A season begins when the land shows it, for example when certain flowers open or certain winds arrive.

perspectives.who: The farmers of ancient Egypt
perspectives.explanation: Three seasons, set by the river Nile: Akhet when the river flooded, Peret when the crops grew, and Shemu when they were harvested.

perspectives.who: The traditional Chinese calendar
perspectives.explanation: Twenty-four short seasons called solar terms, each about 15 days long, with names such as Awakening of Insects and Grain Rain. They are set by the Sun's place on its yearly path. Farmers used them to time each task.

explanations.art: Five wheels of the year side by side, cut into two, three, four, six and twenty-four parts, each with small drawings of rain, flowers, floods, dew and harvest.
explanations.context: This card shows that the number of seasons is something people decide by watching their own land. It is here so that you can question any count, including the one in your schoolbook.

explanations.concept: Festivals follow the Sun: Pongal, Sankranti, Vishu and Onam
explanations.definition: Many festivals mark a point in the Sun's year. Pongal and Makar Sankranti mark the Sun entering the star group Makara, about 14 January. Long ago this was also the day of the December solstice.
explanations.description: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Makar Sankranti across India, Lohri in Punjab and Magh Bihu in Assam all come in mid-January. They thank the Sun as the days begin to lengthen, and they come when the winter harvest is in. But the days really begin to lengthen about 21 December. About 1,700 years ago the two dates matched. Since then the slow wobble of the axis, precession, has shifted the stars behind the Sun. Indian solar calendars follow the stars, so Sankranti moves about one day later every 70 years. Vishu and Puthandu, about 14 April, once marked the March equinox in the same way. Onam in Kerala follows the month of Chingam, in August or September, when the heavy rains ease and the first rice is cut.
examples: Pongal: about 14 January, 24 days after the December solstice.
Vishu, Puthandu, Baisakhi and Poila Boishakh: about 14 or 15 April, 25 days after the March equinox.
Dongzhi in China and Yalda in Iran are kept on the December solstice itself.

perspectives.who: Most Indian panchangam makers
perspectives.explanation: The calendar should follow the stars, as it has for about 2,000 years. Makar Sankranti is the day the Sun enters Makara, wherever the solstice may be. The star-based year keeps festivals tied to the sky that our ancestors named.

perspectives.who: Meghnad Saha and the Calendar Reform Committee, 1952 to 1955
perspectives.explanation: A calendar is for the seasons. The committee found that Indian solar calendars had slipped about 23 days from the seasons. It designed the Indian national calendar, used by the government since 22 March 1957. Its year begins just after the March equinox and stays with the seasons.

explanations.art: A line for the year with 21 December and 14 January marked, a small pot of pongal boiling over at 14 January, and a curved arrow showing the gap of 24 days.
explanations.context: This card joins the science of the orbit to dates your family already keeps, and shows why a calendar tied to the stars slowly slips against the seasons.

explanations.definition: Plants, humans and other animals sense the changing length of the day and the changing weather, and many also carry an inner sense of the year. How these work together is still being studied.
explanations.description: Day length is the steadiest signal of the season, because it repeats exactly every year while heat and rain do not. Many old rice varieties of South India flower only when the days shorten after September, whatever date they were sown. Amur falcons gather in Nagaland in October and November. Then they fly across the Arabian Sea to southern Africa, where summer is beginning. Mango trees flower after the cool, dry weeks of winter. Humans change with the seasons too, in sleep, mood and the food our bodies ask for.
examples: Samba rice in Tamil Nadu is sown in August and flowers as the days shorten.
Amur falcons spend the northern summer in China and Siberia and the southern summer in Africa, so they live in summer for most of the year.
Bar-headed geese cross the Himalaya to winter in Indian lakes such as Koonthankulam and Chilika.

perspectives.who: Eberhard Gwinner, a German scientist, from 1967
perspectives.explanation: Many birds carry an inner yearly clock. He kept warblers and stonechats for years in rooms where day length never changed. The birds still grew restless, put on fat and changed their feathers about once a year. Without the Sun their 'year' slowly drifted to about ten months.

perspectives.who: Field scientists who study plants and insects
perspectives.explanation: Many beings follow the weather of the moment more than any calendar. Desert seeds wait for rain, however long it takes. Mango trees flower early after an early cool spell. For them a season is something that happens, and they answer when it comes.

explanations.art: A flock of small falcons over a reservoir in green hills at dusk, with a faint dotted route leading away over the sea.
explanations.context: This card asks how living beings know what time of year it is. It builds on what you may know about plants measuring the length of the day.

explanations.definition: Any planet with a leaning axis has seasons. The size of the lean and the shape of the orbit decide what the seasons are like.
explanations.description: Mars leans about 25 degrees, close to the Earth's lean. So Mars has four seasons like ours, each about twice as long, because a Mars year is 687 Earth days. Mars's orbit is far more stretched than the Earth's. At its nearest, Mars gets about 45 parts in 100 more sunlight than at its farthest. So on Mars distance really does matter, and southern summers are shorter and hotter than northern ones. Uranus lies almost on its side, leaning about 98 degrees. Each pole has about 42 years of sunlight and then about 42 years of darkness. Jupiter and Venus hardly lean at all, so they have almost no seasons.
examples: Mars: a lean of about 25 degrees and a year of 687 Earth days.
Uranus: a lean of about 98 degrees and a year of 84 Earth years.
Jupiter: a lean of about 3 degrees and almost no seasons.

perspectives.who: A student of the Earth
perspectives.explanation: Distance from the Sun does not make the seasons. Lean does. This is true for the Earth, where the orbit is nearly round.

perspectives.who: A scientist who studies Mars
perspectives.explanation: On a planet with a stretched orbit, both lean and distance make the seasons. Mars's great dust storms tend to begin when Mars is nearest the Sun. The rule 'distance does not matter' belongs to the Earth, not to every planet.

explanations.art: Four planets in a row with their axes drawn: Earth leaning a little, Mars leaning the same, Uranus lying on its side and Jupiter standing straight.
explanations.context: This card tests the idea of this lesson on other worlds. If lean makes seasons, then planets with other leans must have other seasons, and they do.

explanations.concept: Why does the Earth lean at all?
explanations.definition: Nobody saw how the Earth got its lean. The leading idea is that a body about the size of Mars struck the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago, knocked it over and threw out the rock that became the Moon.
explanations.description: William Hartmann and Donald Davis proposed this giant impact in 1975. It explains why Moon rocks are so like the Earth's outer rock. The lean is not fixed. It rocks slowly between about 22 and 24 and a half degrees, once in about 41,000 years. Today it is about 23.4 degrees and getting slowly smaller. A larger lean gives stronger seasons. Scientists also ask what keeps the lean so steady, and here they disagree.
examples: Today's lean: about 23.4 degrees.
The lean changes by less than 3 degrees over 41,000 years.
Mars's lean has swung far more widely in the past than the Earth's.

perspectives.who: Jacques Laskar and his team in Paris, 1993
perspectives.explanation: The Moon holds the Earth's lean steady. Their sums showed that without the Moon, the pulls of the other planets could swing the lean wildly, perhaps from 0 to 85 degrees. Seasons on such an Earth would sometimes be mild and sometimes violent.

perspectives.who: Jack Lissauer, Jason Barnes and John Chambers, 2012
perspectives.explanation: The Moon helps less than was thought. They followed a moonless Earth in a computer for billions of years. Its lean mostly stayed within about 10 degrees of today's value. So a planet may not need a large moon to have steady seasons.

explanations.art: The young Earth being struck a glancing blow by a smaller glowing body, with rock spraying out into a ring.
explanations.context: This card goes to the edge of what is known: where the lean came from and what holds it steady. It is marked as an idea because nobody can go back and look.

agreed.text: Radar and spacecraft give the Sun's distance as about 147.1 million kilometres in early January and about 152.1 million kilometres in early July.
agreed.evidence: Since the 1960s, radar signals have been bounced off Venus and timed. Spacecraft tracking now fixes these distances to within a few metres.

agreed.text: Satellites above the air measure about 7 parts in 100 more sunlight reaching the whole Earth in early January than in early July.
agreed.evidence: Instruments on satellites have recorded the Sun's brightness every day since 1978. The yearly rise and fall matches the changing distance exactly.

agreed.text: A nearby star shifts back and forth against far stars once a year.
agreed.evidence: Friedrich Bessel first measured this shift in 1838, for the star 61 Cygni. The Gaia spacecraft has since measured it for more than a billion stars. It is direct proof that the Earth revolves.

agreed.text: The year of the seasons is 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and about 46 seconds long.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers time the moment of the equinox year after year. Hundreds of years of records give the average.

agreed.text: The Earth's lean is about 23.44 degrees today and is shrinking by about one hundredth of a degree each century.
agreed.evidence: The lean is found from the height of the noon Sun at the two solstices. Records go back more than 2,000 years, to Greek, Chinese and Indian astronomers.

challenging.claim: The seasons come from the Earth's changing distance from the Sun.
challenging.who: A very common belief. In a well-known 1987 film, A Private Universe, most of the new university graduates who were asked could not explain the seasons, and many gave this answer.
challenging.for: A fire feels hotter when we step closer. Schoolbook pictures often show the orbit as a long oval. And the Earth's distance from the Sun really does change.
challenging.against: The Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, in the northern winter. The two hemispheres have opposite seasons on the same day, though they are the same distance from the Sun. And in Lean or Distance, the true change of distance made almost no difference to the light.
challenging.context: This card looks at the most common explanation of the seasons and checks it against three facts.

challenging.claim: Distance still matters a little, even on the Earth.
challenging.who: Milutin Milankovitch in the 1920s, and most climate scientists today
challenging.for: The Earth gets about 7 parts in 100 more sunlight in January than in July. Ice and mud from the deep past show ice ages coming and going in step with slow changes of the orbit and the lean.
challenging.against: Within one year the effect is hard to find. Southern summers are not hotter than northern ones, because the southern half of the Earth is mostly ocean, which warms slowly.
challenging.context: This card stops the lesson from swinging too far. Lean is the main cause of seasons, but distance is not nothing.

challenging.claim: Uttarayana begins on Makar Sankranti, about 14 January.
challenging.who: Most Indian panchangams, which follow the stars
challenging.for: The Sun enters the star group Makara on that day, and the name Uttarayana has been tied to that event for about 2,000 years. A festival is a tradition, and traditions need not move.
challenging.against: The noon Sun turns north about 21 December. Shadow measurements at any Jantar Mantar show it. Meghnad Saha's committee said the calendar should be set right. If nothing changes, Sankranti will keep moving later, into February and one day into summer.
challenging.context: This card is about a live argument in India: should a calendar follow the stars or the seasons?

challenging.claim: The monsoon is a giant sea breeze.
challenging.who: Edmond Halley in 1686, and many schoolbooks since
challenging.for: Land does heat faster than sea, and the winds do blow from sea to land in summer and turn round in winter.
challenging.against: The land is hottest in May, before the rains, and cools once they start, yet the monsoon goes on for months. Sulochana Gadgil showed that the rain belt behaves like the cloud band that circles the Earth near the equator, moved north. Many scientists now use both ideas together.
challenging.context: This card shows that even the cause of India's rains is argued over by scientists today.

challenging.claim: Without the Moon, the Earth's lean would swing wildly and the seasons would be chaos.
challenging.for: Their sums showed the Moon's pull damping the push of the other planets. Mars has only two tiny moons, and its lean has swung by tens of degrees.
challenging.against: In 2012 Jack Lissauer's team ran a moonless Earth in a computer for billions of years and found its lean changed far less than feared. Nobody can test either result on a real planet.
challenging.context: This card asks whether our steady seasons are a gift of the Moon. Two teams of scientists give different answers.

big_questions.q: It is winter in Srinagar and summer in Sydney at the same moment. So what season is the Earth in?
big_questions.hint: Think of The Leaning Ball. Was the whole ball ever in one season? Then ask what the word 'season' is really about.

big_questions.q: In The Leaning Ball, nothing about the ball or the lamp changed. So what was it that changed?
big_questions.hint: Stand where the lamp is, then stand where the ball is. Does the answer depend on where you stand?

big_questions.q: Is a season something in the sky, something in the weather, or something people agree to name?
big_questions.hint: Compare the astronomers' four, the six ritus and the Noongar six. What was each group looking at when they drew the lines?

big_questions.q: If your city needed its own season calendar, how many seasons would you give it, and what would start each one?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you can see, smell and hear changing: a tree, a wind, a fruit in the market, the first rain.

big_questions.q: Should a festival stay on its old star date, or move to stay with the season it once marked?
big_questions.hint: Think of Pongal, 24 days after the shortest day. What would be gained by moving it? What would be lost?

big_questions.q: Would there be as many kinds of living beings on an Earth that stood upright, with no seasons?
big_questions.hint: Think of what seasons make living beings do: travel, store, flower, wait. Then think of the deep sea, where there are almost no seasons.

big_questions.q: People once felt sure that summer meant 'nearer the Sun'. What else do we feel sure about, only because it sounds sensible?
big_questions.hint: Think of how you tested this one. Which of your own sure ideas could be tested with a torch, a ball or a ruler?

open_questions.q: How will India's monsoon change as the Earth warms?
open_questions.why_open: Warmer air holds more water, so most computer models expect heavier bursts of rain. But the models disagree about how the dates, the breaks and the total rain will change, and smoke and dust in the air push the other way.

open_questions.q: Can the start of the monsoon, and the dry breaks inside it, be forecast a month ahead?
open_questions.why_open: Forecasts a few days ahead are now good. Beyond about two weeks they are still weak, because small changes in the ocean and the air grow into large ones. Farmers need exactly this answer.

open_questions.q: How does the inner yearly clock of a bird or a plant work?
open_questions.why_open: The daily body clock is understood down to its genes. No one has yet found how cells count out most of a year. Eberhard Gwinner showed that the clock exists, but its parts are still unknown.

open_questions.q: Did one giant impact really give the Earth its lean?
open_questions.why_open: The impact fits the Moon rocks, but computer models of it give many different leans and spins. Some scientists now propose several smaller impacts. No direct record of the event is left.

open_questions.q: Does a planet need seasons, or steady seasons, for life to spread across it?
open_questions.why_open: We know only one planet with life. Telescopes are just beginning to measure the leans of planets round other stars, so there is nothing yet to compare the Earth with.

story.title: Pongal on the Beach
story.note: A made-up story. Nila, Imran, Appa and Kavitha Chithi are imagined, and so is everything they say and do. The facts in it are real. The Earth is nearest the Sun in early January. Melbourne has summer in January, with daylight until about a quarter to nine at night. Clocks in Melbourne are five and a half hours ahead of clocks in India in January. Chithi is a Tamil word for a mother's younger sister.
text: On Pongal morning the whole lane in Madurai smelled of jaggery and wood smoke. Nila, who was ten, had been up since five. She had drawn a kolam at the door with a Sun in the middle and sugarcane at the corners. The air was cool enough that she had kept her shawl on to draw it.

Now the pongal pot was on the stove in the yard. Appa watched the milk. Imran, who was seven and lived next door, watched Appa. Imran came every year, because Nila's father made the best sakkarai pongal in the lane and Imran's mother made the best biryani, and the two families had an agreement about this.
'Pongalo Pongal!' they all shouted when the milk rose and spilled over the rim.

Then Appa's phone rang. It was Kavitha Chithi, Appa's younger sister, who drove trams in Melbourne in Australia. Her face filled the screen. She wore a big straw hat and dark glasses, and behind her was a bright blue sea.
'Happy Pongal!' said Chithi. 'I am at the beach. It is 36 degrees here. I have eaten two ice creams already.'
'The beach?' said Imran. 'In January? It is cold in January.'
'Not here,' said Chithi. 'Here it is the middle of summer. The Sun will not set until a quarter to nine tonight.'
When the call was over, Imran sat frowning at the kolam. 'I know why,' he said at last. 'Australia is at the bottom of the world. So it must stick out towards the Sun. It is nearer, so it is hotter.'
Nila opened her mouth to agree. It sounded right. Then she stopped. 'Wait,' she said. 'Let us look.'

She took a sweet lime from the Pongal plate and held it near the small lamp that burned beside the pot. 'The lime is the Earth. Here is Madurai, near the top. Here is Melbourne, near the bottom.' She pressed two dots into the peel with her thumbnail. 'Now look from the lamp. Which dot is nearer?'
Imran looked hard. 'They are the same,' he said. 'Almost.'

'And the real Sun is very, very far,' said Nila. 'Miss told us. If the Earth were this lime, the Sun would be nearly a kilometre away, and as tall as a two-storey house. The top and the bottom of the lime are the same distance from something that far off.'
Appa looked up from the pot. 'There was something in the paper last week,' he said. 'It said the Earth was at its closest to the Sun for the whole year. On the third of January.'
'Closest? Now?' said Nila. 'But I wore a shawl this morning. And Delhi has fog, and the news showed snow in Kashmir.'
'That is what it said,' said Appa. 'I did not understand it either.'

So it could not be nearness. The whole Earth was near the Sun this month, and half of it was cold. Nila turned the lime in her fingers. There had to be something that was different for Madurai and Melbourne on the same day.
'It leans,' she said slowly. 'The globe at school leans. I thought it was only made like that so we could see India.'
She tilted the lime so that the stalk end leaned away from the lamp. 'Look now, Imran. Do not look at how near. Look at how the light lands.'
Imran bent close. On the Melbourne dot the lamplight fell straight and bright. On the Madurai dot it came in sideways and thin, stretched over the curve of the peel.
'Chithi is getting it full in the face,' said Imran. 'We are getting it from the side.'

'Now I walk to the other side of the lamp,' said Nila. 'That is six months. I must not turn the stalk. It keeps pointing at the gate.' She carried the lime round to the far side, with the stalk still leaning towards the gate. Now the stalk end leaned in towards the lamp. The light fell straight on the Madurai dot and thin on the Melbourne dot.
'May,' said Appa. 'When even the crows sit with their beaks open.'
'So Chithi will be cold in June,' said Imran, 'and she will ring us and we will be the ones eating ice cream.' He was very pleased with this.
They ate the pongal sitting on the step. The Sun was well up now, and the shawl lay folded beside Nila.
'Appa,' she said, 'Pongal is for thanking the Sun for coming back north. Paatti used to say so.'
'She did.'
'But the Sun did not go anywhere. We leaned.' She thought about it. 'And we did not even change our lean. We only went round to the other side.'
Imran licked his fingers. 'Then who do we thank?' he asked.
Nobody answered straight away. A crow landed on the wall and looked at the pot with one eye.
'One more thing,' said Imran. 'If Chithi has summer now and we have winter now, what does the Earth have?'
Nila looked at the sweet lime in her hand, half in the lamplight and half out of it. She did not know yet. She put it back on the plate, leaning.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Nila stops looking at how near each dot is to the lamp and looks at how the light lands on it. Both dots are the same distance away, and the whole Earth is nearest the Sun in January. What differs is the slant. The second turn is her own: the lean never changed, they only went round to the other side.
ask: Why did Nila ask Imran to look at how the light lands, and not at how near the dots were?
Why did the stalk of the lime have to keep pointing at the gate?
Imran asked: if it is summer and winter at the same time, what does the Earth have? What do you think?
Nila said the Sun did not come back, and that they had only gone round to the other side. Then who, or what, would you thank at Pongal?
