how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that the calendar of the stars and the calendar of the seasons slowly drift apart? This card tells the true story, from a Greek island to India's own calendar.
how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people in India, Babylon, Egypt and Greece told the seasons by the stars. When a certain star rose before dawn, it was time to sow. They believed that the Sun came back to the same stars each time the same season came back. It fitted everything a person could see in one lifetime. About 127 BCE, the Greek astronomer Hipparchus compared his own measurement of the bright star Spica with one made about 160 years earlier by Timocharis. Spica had shifted by about 2 degrees from the place of the September equinox. The star year and the season year were not the same length. They differ by about 20 minutes. In one lifetime that is nothing. In 1,700 years it is more than three weeks. In 1952 the physicist Meghnad Saha led a committee to study India's many calendars. It found that Makar Sankranti had slipped about 23 days from the December solstice it once marked. The committee designed a national calendar that follows the seasons.
how_we_found_out.who: Timocharis of Alexandria, Hipparchus of Nicaea, and Meghnad Saha with the Calendar Reform Committee of India
how_we_found_out.when: Timocharis measured Spica about 290 BCE and Hipparchus about 127 BCE. Saha's committee worked from 1952 to 1955, and the Indian national calendar began on 22 March 1957.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Sun returns to the same stars each time the same season returns, so a calendar tied to the stars will stay with the seasons for ever. Hipparchus showed, from a star that had shifted in 160 years, that the two slowly drift apart.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in ancient Greek dress on a flat roof at night, sighting a bright star along a wooden rod, with an old scroll of numbers open beside a small oil lamp.

roots.context: We have learned that a steady lean, carried round the Sun, gives summer and winter. Now we ask what this tells us about change, about opposites and about where we stand.

deep_truth.truth: In The Leaning Ball, the lean of the ball never changed. Its top dot pointed at the same wall all the way round the lamp. Yet the northern ring went from nine lit dots to three, while the southern ring went from three to nine. So summer and winter are not two things that take turns. They are one steady lean, lit from one side, and both are always here.
deep_truth.habit: We think that a change in what we feel must come from a change in the thing that causes it. So we say that summer 'comes' and winter 'goes', as if heat were sent to us and taken away. And we treat summer and winter as opposites, when they are the two ends of one leaning ball on the same day.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Leaning Ball, the lamp and the lean stayed the same at all four places, and only our place on the circle changed. In Lean or Distance, moving the torch as the Earth really moves made almost no difference. And the Earth is nearest the Sun in January, when the north is cold and the south is hot.

three.who_am_i: You are standing on a leaning, spinning ball, and what you call 'this season' is your place on it. A child in Sydney, on the same ball on the same day, is living your opposite.
three.what_is_life: Living beings do not wait for the seasons to happen to them. Rice, falcons, mango trees and humans read the light and the rain and move with them. Some carry the year inside their own bodies.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is not hot in one season and cold in another. It is always both. The rains, the harvests and the festivals all come from one lean that has hardly changed since before there were humans.

roots.thread: The Sun gives the same light all year. The Earth keeps the same lean all year. Out of these two steady things come the monsoon, the mango season, the falcons' journey, Pongal, Onam and the six ritus. The many seasons of the many peoples are one lean, seen from different places on one ball.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that the touch of the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and they go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them steadily.
teachings.link: The Gita names heat and cold as the first example of things that come and go. In The Leaning Ball you saw why they come and go, and what stays steady while they do.

teachings.source: Heraclitus of Ephesus, fragment B67 in the Diels-Kranz numbering, about 500 BCE
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus wrote that the divine is day and night, winter and summer, war and peace, plenty and hunger. It takes different forms, as a fire takes the scent of whatever spice is thrown on it.
teachings.link: He put winter and summer together as two faces of one thing. On the leaning ball they are exactly that: the two ends of one lean, at the same moment.

teachings.teaching: This old Indian text sorts the six seasons into two sets of three. It ties one set to the half of the year when the Sun moves north, and the other set to the half when the Sun moves south.
teachings.link: More than 2,500 years ago, people in India had already seen that the seasons follow the Sun's swing north and south. The leaning ball shows what makes the swing.

science.text: The Earth's seasons come from the lean of its axis, not from its distance from the Sun. The Earth is nearest the Sun in early January.
The Earth's lean came from a giant impact about 4.5 billion years ago.
The Moon is what keeps the Earth's lean, and so its seasons, steady.
How living beings keep an inner count of the year.

other_view.view: Something does change through the year: the direction from the Earth to the Sun. To say the cause is 'steady' is only to choose the Sun's point of view. And for a mango tree or a farmer, summer and winter are truly different times that follow each other. It does not help them to be told that both are always here somewhere else.

practice.title: Lean into the light
practice.say: Sit sideways to a window or a lamp, an arm's length away. Close your eyes. Turn your face slowly towards the light as you breathe in. Feel it land full on your cheeks. Turn slowly away as you breathe out. Feel the light thin out on one cheek. The lamp has not changed. Only your lean has changed. Do this five times.
practice.kid: Sit near a window or a lamp. Close your eyes. Turn your face to the light as you breathe in. Turn away as you breathe out. Feel the light change on your cheek. The light is the same. Only you moved.

ask: In The Leaning Ball, the lamp and the lean stayed the same, yet you counted summer and winter. Where did the change come from?
Is there anything in your own life that feels as if it comes and goes, when really you are the one who has moved?
A child in Sydney is living the opposite of your season today. Are the two of you in two different worlds, or in one?
roots.art: A leaning ball beside a small lamp, the top half bright and the bottom half dim, with a tiny child standing on the bright part and another tiny child standing on the dim part, both waving.

experiments.title: Lean or Distance: which one changes the light more?
experiments.context: In this experiment a torch is the Sun and a white card is the ground. You change the distance as the Earth's distance really changes, and you lean the card as Chennai and Delhi really lean. Then you see which change matters more.
experiments.question: Between January and July the Earth moves about 3 parts in 100 further from the Sun. Between June and December the ground in Delhi leans about 47 degrees further from the noon Sun. Which of these two changes spreads the light more?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Which will change the patch of light more: moving the torch from 30 cm to 31 cm, or leaning the card back as Delhi leans in December? Or will they be about equal? Write your guess and the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same torch, the same tube and the same card all through. In the lean test, only the lean of the card changes, and the dot on the card stays 30 cm from the torch. In the distance test, only the distance changes, and the card stays upright. Measure every patch twice, because the edge of a torch patch is soft.
results_table: My guess: more, less or same light on each square
Upright length divided by this length

materials.item: a torch. A phone torch also works.
a cardboard tube about 15 cm long, such as the inside of a kitchen roll. A sheet of chart paper rolled and taped also works.
a stiff card about the size of a notebook, such as the back cover of an old notebook
white paper to cover the card, and cello tape
a 30 cm ruler and a pencil
a protractor from a geometry box. With no protractor, use the lean distances given in step 3.
a pile of books to rest the torch on, and one heavy book to prop the card
a room you can make dark, at night or with the curtains closed

schedule.what: Set up the torch and the card. Guess. Lean the card to four settings, then move the torch 1 cm. Measure each patch twice and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences: what I think (my claim), what I saw (my evidence), and why I think it happened (my reasoning). Keep the white paper with the pencil outlines on it.

setup.art: A torch with a cardboard tube taped over its front, lying on a pile of books and pointing sideways at a white card that stands upright 30 cm away.
setup.caption: 1. Rest the torch on books. Stand the white card upright, 30 cm in front of it.

setup.art: The same card leaning back away from the torch, with a protractor at its foot and the round patch of light stretched into a tall oval.
setup.caption: 2. Lean the card back. Slide it so the pencil dot is still 30 cm from the torch.

setup.art: A child's hands holding a ruler against the card, measuring the oval patch of light from its top edge to its bottom edge.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the patch from top to bottom, twice.

setup.art: The card upright again with the torch pulled back by 1 cm along a ruler lying on the table.
setup.caption: 4. For the distance test, stand the card upright and move the torch back 1 cm.

flow.do: 1. Tape white paper over the card. Mark a pencil dot in its middle. 2. Tape the tube over the front of the torch, so the beam is narrow. 3. Lay the torch on the books, pointing sideways. 4. Stand the card upright, facing the torch, with the dot 30 cm from the end of the tube. Prop it with the heavy book. 5. Make the room dark. Move the torch until the patch is centred on the dot.
flow.say: The torch is our Sun and the card is the ground. When the card stands upright, the light hits it straight on. That is the Sun exactly overhead.
flow.kid: Cover the card with white paper. Mark a dot in the middle. Put the tube on the torch. Stand the card 30 cm away. Make the room dark.
flow.parent: The patch should be a clear round shape about 5 to 8 cm wide. If it is wider than the card, move everything to 20 cm and use 20 cm wherever the steps say 30. A phone torch gives a softer edge. That is fine, as long as your child draws the edge the same way each time.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lean or Distance. You set up a torch as the Sun and a white card as the ground, 30 cm apart.

flow.do: 1. Read the question aloud. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guess in the table for each setting.
flow.say: The Earth is about 3 parts in 100 further from the Sun in July than in January. Here that is 1 cm in 30. In Delhi the noon Sun is 5 degrees from overhead in June and 52 degrees in December. Which change will spread the light more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which spreads the light more: moving the torch 1 cm, or leaning the card? Guess. Say why.

ask.q: Which will change the patch more, and why do you think so?
good: Distance, because things are hotter when you are closer.
Lean, because the light will be stretched out.
Any guess with a reason. The test will decide.

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Most children, and most grown-ups, guess distance. Write the guess down so you can come back to it.
flow.context: This is the guessing step of Lean or Distance. You guess whether distance or lean changes the patch of light more, before you measure.

flow.do: 1. With the card upright, your child draws round the edge of the patch and measures it from top to bottom. Write it down as lean 0. 2. Lean the card back 10 degrees from upright. Use the protractor at the foot of the card. 3. Slide the card until the dot is again 30 cm from the tube and the patch is centred on it. 4. Draw round the patch and measure its length from top to bottom. 5. Do the same at 37 degrees. 6. Measure each patch a second time.
flow.say: Ten degrees is the noon Sun in Chennai in June. Thirty-seven degrees is the noon Sun in Chennai in December. Watch the shape of the patch as the card leans.
flow.kid: Measure the patch with the card upright. Lean the card back 10 degrees. Measure again. Then lean it 37 degrees. Measure again.
flow.parent: With no protractor, use a card 20 cm tall and measure how far its top edge has moved back from upright: 3.5 cm for 10 degrees, 12 cm for 37 degrees, 1.7 cm for 5 degrees and 16 cm for 52 degrees. One person holds the card steady while the other draws. The width of the patch stays the same. Only its length grows. With a 6 cm patch, expect about 6.1 cm at 10 degrees and about 7.5 cm at 37 degrees.
flow.context: This is the Chennai step of Lean or Distance. You lean the card as the ground in Chennai leans from the noon Sun in June and in December.

flow.do: 1. Lean the card back 5 degrees, slide it so the dot is 30 cm away, and measure the patch. 2. Do the same at 52 degrees. 3. Measure each a second time.
flow.say: Five degrees is the noon Sun in Delhi in June. Fifty-two degrees is the noon Sun in Delhi in December. Is Delhi's change bigger or smaller than Chennai's?
flow.kid: Lean the card 5 degrees and measure. Lean it 52 degrees and measure. Is Delhi's change bigger than Chennai's?
flow.parent: With a 6 cm patch, expect about 6 cm at 5 degrees and about 9.7 cm at 52 degrees. At 52 degrees the patch may run off a small card. Then move the card so the whole patch fits, keeping the dot at 30 cm.
flow.context: This is the Delhi step of Lean or Distance. You lean the card as the ground in Delhi leans from the noon Sun in June and in December.

flow.do: 1. Stand the card upright again with the dot 30 cm from the tube. 2. Measure the width of the patch as carefully as you can, to the nearest millimetre. 3. Move the torch back exactly 1 cm, so the dot is 31 cm away. 4. Measure the width again. 5. Do both a second time.
flow.say: Now the distance test. Thirty centimetres is the Earth in January. Thirty-one is the Earth in July. Measure very carefully, because the change may be small.
flow.kid: Stand the card upright. Measure the patch at 30 cm. Move the torch back 1 cm. Measure again, very carefully.
flow.parent: Expect the patch to grow by about 2 mm, for example from 6.0 cm to 6.2 cm. Many families cannot see any change at all. That is a real result, so write it down as it is.
flow.context: This is the distance step of Lean or Distance. You move the torch 1 cm further away, as the Earth moves between January and July.

flow.do: 1. For each setting, divide the upright length by the measured length. 2. Write the answer in the last column. It tells you what share of the straight-on light each square centimetre now gets. 3. Put the six settings in order, from the most light on each square to the least.
flow.say: The same light is now spread over a longer patch. If the patch is twice as long, each square gets half the light. Which setting gave each square the least light?
flow.kid: Divide the upright length by each new length. A smaller answer means less light on each square. Which setting is lowest?

ask.q: Which change spread the light more: 1 cm of distance, or Delhi's December lean?
good: The lean, by far. The patch was more than one and a half times as long.
The distance hardly changed the patch at all.

flow.parent: Worked example with a 6 cm patch: at 37 degrees, 6 divided by 7.5 is 0.8. At 52 degrees, 6 divided by 9.7 is about 0.6. For the distance test the patch grows in width and in height, so the share is about 0.93. Chennai in December still gets 8 parts in 10 of the straight-on light. Delhi gets only 6 parts in 10.

check.q: In December each square of Delhi ground gets about 6 parts in 10 of June's noon light. Why?
options: Delhi is further from the Sun in December
The same light is spread over a longer patch
The Sun gives less light in December
Clouds block the light in December
check.why: Slanting light is spread over more ground. The whole Earth is in fact nearest the Sun in early January, and the Sun gives the same light all year. If you chose distance, look again at your 31 cm result.

flow.context: This is the working-out step of Lean or Distance. You turn each patch length into the share of light that reaches each square of the card.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 2. Go back to the guess from step 2 and compare. 3. Then tell your child when the Earth is nearest the Sun, and talk about what this test leaves out.
flow.say: Write what you think now, what you saw, and why. Then here is a fact. The Earth is nearest the Sun in early January. Does that fit your result? What does our torch test leave out?
flow.kid: Write your claim, your evidence and your reason. The Earth is nearest the Sun in January. Does that fit what you found?
flow.think: A torch beam spreads out, but sunlight arrives almost as straight, side-by-side rays. Does that make our distance test too strong or too weak?
flow.parent: The test leaves out three things. Real sunlight hardly spreads at all, so distance matters even less than the torch shows. Slanting sunlight also crosses more air. And summer days are longer, which adds to the heating. The Leaning Ball looks at the longer days.
flow.context: This is the last step of Lean or Distance. You write what you found, compare it with your guess, and ask what the test cannot show.

experiments.title: The Leaning Ball: would an upright Earth have seasons?
experiments.context: In this experiment a ball with pen dots is the Earth and a lamp is the Sun. You carry the ball to four places round the lamp, first leaning and then upright. At each place you count how many dots on a northern ring and a southern ring are in the light.
experiments.question: How many hours of daylight does a far northern place get at four points of the year, and a far southern place? What happens to the count if the Earth stands upright?
experiments.predict: Each ring has 12 dots, and each dot stands for 2 hours of the day. Guess how many dots will be lit on the northern ring at each of the four places, with the ball leaning. Then guess for the ball standing upright. Give a reason for each guess.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ball, the same lamp and the same four places, each 60 cm from the lamp. With the leaning ball, the top dot must lean towards the same wall at every place. In the second round only one thing changes: the ball stands upright. Count each ring twice, once from each side.
results_table: Leaning: lit dots on the northern ring
Leaning: lit dots on the southern ring
Upright: lit dots on the northern ring
Upright: lit dots on the southern ring
Hours of daylight in the north (lit dots times 2)

materials.item: a pale ball about 7 cm wide, such as a sweet lime, an orange or a tennis ball
rubber bands that fit snugly round the ball
a sketch pen, and a small sticker or a dab of kumkum for the top dot
steel tumblers, one for the ball to sit on and one for the lamp
a small lamp with a bare bulb, or a phone torch that you turn to face the ball at each place
a ruler, paper and cello tape to mark four places on the floor or on a large table
a room you can make dark

schedule.what: Mark the ball and the four places. Guess. Count lit dots at four places with the ball leaning, then with the ball upright. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the lamp and the four places seen from above, with the lean of the ball shown at each place. Then write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: lit dots on the northern ring, ball leaning
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your counts may differ by one dot.

setup.art: A sweet lime with three rubber bands: one round its middle, one two-thirds of the way up and one two-thirds of the way down, with pen dots along the upper and lower bands and a red dot on top.
setup.caption: 1. Put one band round the middle and one band two-thirds of the way to each end. Mark 12 dots along the upper and the lower band.

setup.art: A view from above of a lamp on an upturned tumbler in the middle of a floor, with four paper marks numbered 1 to 4 round it, each 60 cm away.
setup.caption: 2. Mark four places round the lamp, each 60 cm from it.

setup.art: The ball sitting on a tumbler at place 1, leaning so that its red top dot tips towards the lamp, with the lit side facing the lamp.
setup.caption: 3. At place 1 the top dot leans towards the lamp. It leans towards that same wall at every other place.

setup.art: A child crouching beside the ball in a dark room, counting the pen dots on the upper band that are in the light.
setup.caption: 4. Count the dots that are in the light on each ring.

flow.do: 1. Put one rubber band round the middle of the ball. This is the equator. 2. Mark the top with a sticker. This is the North Pole. 3. Put a second band two-thirds of the way from the equator to the North Pole. Put a third band two-thirds of the way to the other end. 4. With the sketch pen, mark 12 dots along the northern band, evenly spaced. Mark the 4 quarter points first, then 2 more in each gap. 5. Do the same along the southern band.
flow.say: This ball is the Earth. The middle band is the equator. The upper band is a ring of places far in the north, like Norway. The lower band is far in the south. As the Earth spins, a place travels once round its ring in 24 hours. So each of the 12 dots is 2 hours.
flow.kid: Put a band round the middle. Put a band near each end. Mark 12 dots along each end band. Mark the top with a sticker.
flow.parent: Two-thirds of the way to the pole is 60 degrees north. The rings are far north and far south so that the change is big enough to count. India lies much nearer the equator, where the change is real but too small to count with 12 dots.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Leaning Ball. You turn a ball into a model Earth with an equator and two rings of 12 dots.

flow.do: 1. Stand the lamp on an upturned tumbler in the middle of the floor. 2. Mark four places round it with paper and tape, each 60 cm from the lamp. Number them 1 to 4, going round anticlockwise as seen from above. 3. Choose the wall that place 1 faces across the lamp. Call it the lean wall. 4. Ask for the guesses and write them down.
flow.say: The ball will sit on a tumbler at each place. Its top will always lean towards the lean wall, about a quarter of the way from standing to lying. How many northern dots will be lit at each place? And if the ball stands upright? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mark four places round the lamp. Pick one wall as the lean wall. Guess the lit dots at each place. Say why.

ask.q: Will the count of lit dots be the same at all four places, and why do you think so?
good: No. When the top leans to the lamp, more of the top ring will be in the light.
Yes, because half the ball is always lit.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.parent: Place 1 is the place where the top dot leans towards the lamp. So the lean wall is the wall behind the lamp as seen from place 1. A quarter of the way from standing to lying is about 23 degrees. The lamp must be level with the middle of the ball.
flow.context: This is the guessing step of The Leaning Ball. You mark four places round the lamp and guess how many dots will be lit at each.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Sit the ball on its tumbler at place 1, with the top leaning towards the lean wall. 3. Your child counts the dots in the light on the northern ring, then on the southern ring. A dot on the edge of the light counts as half. 4. Carry the ball to place 2. Do not turn it. The top must still lean towards the lean wall. Count again. 5. Do the same at places 3 and 4.
flow.say: Half of the ball is always lit. But is half of each ring lit? Count the dots in the light. Keep the top leaning to the same wall at every place.
flow.kid: Put the leaning ball at place 1. Count the lit dots on each ring. Carry it to the next place. Keep the top leaning to the same wall.
flow.parent: Expect about 9 and 3 at place 1, about 6 and 6 at places 2 and 4, and about 3 and 9 at place 3. One dot either way is fine. The usual slip is to turn the ball so that it keeps leaning towards the lamp. Check the top dot against the lean wall each time. With a phone torch, turn the torch to face the ball at each place.
flow.context: This is the first counting step of The Leaning Ball. You count the lit dots on both rings at four places, with the ball leaning the same way each time.

flow.do: 1. Now stand the ball upright on its tumbler, with the top dot pointing at the ceiling. 2. Count the lit dots on both rings at all four places.
flow.say: Now the Earth stands straight up. Nothing else has changed. Count again at each place.
flow.kid: Stand the ball upright. Count the lit dots on each ring at all four places.
flow.parent: Expect about 6 and 6 at every place. An upright Earth has 12 hours of day and 12 of night everywhere, all year.
flow.context: This is the second counting step of The Leaning Ball. You stand the ball upright and count the lit dots again at the same four places.

flow.do: 1. Multiply each northern count by 2 to get hours of daylight. 2. Ask which place is the June solstice, which is the December solstice and which two are the equinoxes. 3. Look at the leaning counts for north and south side by side.
flow.say: Each dot is two hours. Which place gave the north its longest day? Which gave the south its longest day? What do you notice when you put the two columns side by side?
flow.kid: Multiply each count by 2 to get hours. Which place is June? Which is December? Compare north and south.

ask.q: What do you notice about the north and the south at place 1 and at place 3?
good: When the north has the most lit dots, the south has the fewest.
They swap. The seasons are opposite.

check.q: The ball leaned the same way at every place. So why did the count change?
options: The lamp grew brighter at place 1
The ball was nearer the lamp at place 1
The light met the same lean from a different side
The ball spun faster at place 1
check.why: The lean never changed, and every place was 60 cm from the lamp. Only the side the light came from changed. If you chose 'nearer', measure the four distances again.

flow.context: This is the working-out step of The Leaning Ball. You turn dots into hours and match the four places to the solstices and equinoxes.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 2. Compare with the guesses from step 2. 3. Talk about what the model leaves out.
flow.say: Would an upright Earth have seasons? Write what you think, what you counted, and why. Then tell me one way our ball is not like the real Earth.
flow.kid: Would an upright Earth have seasons? Write your claim, your evidence and your reason.
flow.think: What would you count if the ball lay flat on its side, like the planet Uranus?
flow.parent: The model leaves out the air, the oceans and the clouds, which move heat about. The real Sun is also much further away for its size, so real sunlight lights almost exactly half the Earth. Our lamp lights a little less than half.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Leaning Ball. You write what you found and say what the model cannot show.

experiments.safety: Use a lamp with an LED bulb, which stays cool. An old-style bulb gets hot enough to burn, so do not touch it.

experiments.title: Four Cities, Two Days: where does the length of the day change most?
experiments.context: In this investigation you use real sunrise and sunset times for four Indian cities, from the far south to the far north. You work out the length of the longest day and the shortest day in each, and look for a pattern.
experiments.question: Is the difference between the longest day and the shortest day the same all over India? If not, where is it biggest, and how does it grow as you go north?
experiments.predict: The four cities are Kanyakumari, Chennai, Delhi and Srinagar. Guess how much longer 21 June is than 21 December in each city, in hours and minutes. Do you expect the difference to grow evenly as you go north? Give your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same two dates for every city: 21 June and 21 December. Use times from one source, all in Indian clock time. Work out every day length the same way: sunset time minus sunrise time.
results_table: City and how far north it is

materials.item: the table of Sun times in step 2
paper, a pencil and a ruler
squared paper from a maths notebook, for the bar chart
a map of India or a globe, if you have one

schedule.what: Guess. Work out eight day lengths and four differences from the Sun times. Draw a bar chart and look for the pattern.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with two bars for each city, one for June and one for December. Then write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

setup.art: A map of India with four dots from bottom to top labelled Kanyakumari, Chennai, Delhi and Srinagar.
setup.caption: 1. Find the four cities on a map, from south to north.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of sunrise and sunset times and a child working out one day length beside it.
setup.caption: 2. For each city and each date, take the sunrise time away from the sunset time.

setup.art: A bar chart on squared paper with four pairs of bars, the pairs growing more unequal from left to right.
setup.caption: 3. Draw two bars for each city and compare.

flow.do: 1. Find the four cities on a map. Kanyakumari is about 8 degrees north of the equator, Chennai 13, Delhi 29 and Srinagar 34. 2. Ask for a guess for each city and a reason. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: On 21 June the days are longest all over India. On 21 December they are shortest. How big is the difference in each city? Does it grow evenly as we go north? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find the four cities on a map. Guess how much longer June's day is in each. Say why.

ask.q: Where will the difference be biggest, and why do you think so?
good: In Srinagar, because it is furthest from the equator.
The same everywhere, because it is one country under one Sun.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.context: This is the guessing step of Four Cities, Two Days. You guess how much the length of the day changes in four Indian cities.

flow.do: 1. Copy these times. Kanyakumari: 21 June, sunrise 6:03 and sunset 6:39. 21 December, sunrise 6:28 and sunset 6:07. 2. Chennai: 21 June, 5:43 and 6:37. 21 December, 6:26 and 5:47. 3. Delhi: 21 June, 5:23 and 7:22. 21 December, 7:09 and 5:29. 4. Srinagar: 21 June, 5:19 and 7:45. 21 December, 7:32 and 5:25. 5. Your child works out each day length. Count from sunrise up to 12 noon, then add the time from noon to sunset.
flow.say: All sunrises are in the morning and all sunsets are in the evening. Work out how long the Sun is up each time. Start with Chennai in June.
flow.kid: Copy the times. For each one, count from sunrise to noon. Then add noon to sunset. That is the day length.
flow.parent: Answers, for June and then December. Kanyakumari: 12 hours 36 minutes and 11 hours 39 minutes. Chennai: 12 hours 54 minutes and 11 hours 21 minutes. Delhi: 13 hours 59 minutes and 10 hours 20 minutes. Srinagar: 14 hours 26 minutes and 9 hours 53 minutes. The times are rounded to the minute and can differ by a minute or two from a newspaper.
flow.context: This is the working-out step of Four Cities, Two Days. You turn eight pairs of sunrise and sunset times into day lengths.

flow.do: 1. Take each December length away from the June length. 2. Draw a bar chart with two bars for each city. Let one square stand for one hour.
flow.say: Now find the difference for each city. Then draw the bars side by side, south to north. What shape do the pairs of bars make?
flow.kid: Take December's length from June's length for each city. Draw two bars for each city.
flow.parent: Differences: Kanyakumari 57 minutes, Chennai 1 hour 33 minutes, Delhi 3 hours 39 minutes, Srinagar 4 hours 33 minutes.
flow.context: This is the chart step of Four Cities, Two Days. You find the four differences and draw them as pairs of bars.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 2. Compare with the guesses. 3. Look at the sunrise times once more. In which month does Delhi see the Sun before Kanyakumari?
flow.say: What pattern do you see? Write your claim, your evidence and your reason. Then look again at the sunrise times. Something odd happens between June and December.
flow.kid: Write what you found and why. Then look at the sunrise times in Delhi and Kanyakumari. What swaps?
flow.think: At the equator the difference is almost nothing, and at the North Pole it is the whole 24 hours. What would you expect for a city halfway between Srinagar and the Pole?

check.q: A city is on the equator. How much longer is its day on 21 June than on 21 December?
check.why: The difference shrinks as you go south: about 4 and a half hours in Srinagar and under 1 hour in Kanyakumari. At the equator every day is close to 12 hours. If you chose a larger number, look at how your four bars change from north to south.

flow.parent: In June the Sun rises in Delhi 40 minutes before it rises in Kanyakumari. In December it rises in Kanyakumari 41 minutes before Delhi. The line between night and day leans across India one way in June and the other way in December. The differences do not grow evenly. They grow faster and faster towards the pole.
flow.context: This is the last step of Four Cities, Two Days. You write the pattern you found and spot a swap in the sunrise times.

activities.title: The True Shape of the Year: draw the Earth's path to scale
activities.context: This activity starts the lesson. You draw the Earth's path round the Sun at its true shape, mark the nearest and farthest points, and meet a surprise in the dates.

materials.item: a round steel plate or lid about 20 cm wide
a sheet of plain paper larger than the plate
a sharpened pencil and a 30 cm ruler

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Write on it the two distances, the two dates, and one thing you now wonder about.

setup.art: A child drawing round a steel plate on a sheet of paper with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round the plate to make the Earth's path.

setup.art: The drawn circle with two ruler lines crossing at its centre and a small dot a tiny step to one side of the crossing.
setup.caption: 2. Find the centre. Mark the Sun 2 mm to one side of it.

setup.art: A ruler lying across the circle through the Sun dot, with the short side labelled January and the long side labelled July.
setup.caption: 3. Measure from the Sun to the nearest and the farthest points of the path.

flow.do: 1. Give your child a scrap of paper. 2. Ask them to draw, from memory, the path the Earth takes round the Sun. 3. Ask them to mark where the Earth is when India has summer.
flow.say: Draw the Earth's path round the Sun as you picture it. Put the Sun in. Then mark where the Earth is in our summer. Why did you put it there?
flow.kid: Draw the Earth's path round the Sun from memory. Mark where the Earth is in summer. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you put summer there?
good: Because the Earth is closer to the Sun there.
I am not sure.
Any reason. Keep the drawing to look at later.

flow.parent: Many children draw a long oval with the Sun in the middle and put summer at a near point. Do not correct it. Keep the scrap.
flow.context: This is the first step of The True Shape of the Year. You draw the Earth's path as you picture it, before you see the real shape.

flow.do: 1. Draw round the plate on the large sheet. 2. Measure the widest line across the circle and draw it. Turn the ruler a quarter turn and draw the widest line again. The centre is where the lines cross. 3. Mark a dot 2 mm from the centre along one line. This dot is the Sun.
flow.say: This circle is the true shape of the Earth's path, as near as a pencil can draw it. The real path is an ellipse, but the stretch is thinner than your pencil line. The Sun is not quite at the centre. It is 2 millimetres off.
flow.kid: Draw round the plate. Find the centre with two ruler lines. Mark the Sun 2 mm from the centre.
flow.parent: On a path 20 cm wide, the true gap between the centre and the Sun is 1.7 mm. The path itself is narrower one way than the other by much less than the width of a hair.
flow.context: This is the drawing step of The True Shape of the Year. You draw the Earth's path to scale and put the Sun in its true place.

flow.do: 1. Measure from the Sun dot to the nearest point of the circle, along the line. 2. Measure to the farthest point. 3. On this drawing, 1 cm stands for 15 million km. Label the near point '3 January, 147 million km' and the far point '4 July, 152 million km'.
flow.say: Measure from the Sun to the nearest point and to the farthest point. One centimetre here is 15 million kilometres. Now write in the real dates.
flow.kid: Measure from the Sun to the nearest point. Then to the farthest point. Write in the dates and distances.
flow.parent: Expect about 9.8 cm and 10.2 cm. Times 15, these give 147 and 153 million km, which is right to within the width of a pencil line.
flow.context: This is the measuring step of The True Shape of the Year. You measure the nearest and farthest distances and label them with their real dates.

flow.do: 1. Put the scrap drawing beside the true one. 2. Ask what your child notices and what they wonder. Write one wonder on the drawing.
flow.say: Look at the two drawings side by side. What do you notice? Look at the dates. When is the Earth nearest the Sun? What do you wonder now?
flow.kid: Put your two drawings side by side. What is different? When is the Earth nearest the Sun? What do you wonder?
flow.think: If nearness does not make summer, what else could be different between June and December?
flow.parent: Do not explain yet. The wonder you hope for is: 'Then why is January cold?' Lean or Distance answers it.
flow.context: This is the last step of The True Shape of the Year. You compare your first drawing with the true shape and say what puzzles you.

activities.title: Zero Shadow Hunt: when is the Sun exactly overhead in your city?
activities.context: In this activity you use a table of dates to find the two zero shadow days of your own city, or to show that it has none. Then you work out which way noon shadows point in between.

materials.item: the list of cities and the table of dates in steps 1 and 2
paper and a pencil
a calendar for this year
a steel tumbler and a sunny floor at noon, for the extra step only

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun, on a zero shadow day or on any other day. Look only at the shadow on the floor.
activities.record: Write your city, how far north it is, and its two zero shadow dates. Mark them on the family calendar. Draw a noon shadow for January, for the first zero shadow day and for 21 June.

setup.art: A map of India with a dotted line across the middle labelled Tropic of Cancer, and cities marked above and below it.
setup.caption: 1. Find your city and how many degrees north it is.

setup.art: A wall calendar with two dates circled in red, one in April and one in August.
setup.caption: 2. Read your two dates from the table and circle them.

setup.art: A steel tumbler standing in bright sunlight on a terrace floor at noon, with no shadow to be seen round its base.
setup.caption: 3. On that day at local noon, an upright tumbler has no shadow.

flow.do: 1. Find your city, or the nearest one, in this list of degrees north. Kanyakumari 8. Thiruvananthapuram 8 and a half. Kochi and Madurai 10. Coimbatore 11. Bengaluru, Chennai and Mangaluru 13. Panaji 15 and a half. Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam 17 and a half. Pune 18 and a half. Mumbai 19. Bhubaneswar 20. Nagpur 21. Kolkata 22 and a half. Ahmedabad and Bhopal 23. 2. These cities are north of the Tropic of Cancer: Imphal 25, Patna 25 and a half, Guwahati 26, Jaipur and Lucknow 27, Delhi 28 and a half, Srinagar 34. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: On a zero shadow day the noon Sun is exactly overhead. Does our city have such a day? How many each year? In which months? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find your city in the list. Does the Sun ever stand exactly overhead there? Guess when. Say why.

ask.q: How many zero shadow days does our city have in a year, and why do you think so?
good: Two, once when the Sun is going north and once when it comes back.
None, because we are north of the Tropic of Cancer.
One, on 21 June. (This is true only on the Tropic itself.)

flow.context: This is the first step of Zero Shadow Hunt. You find how far north your city is and guess whether the Sun is ever overhead there.

flow.do: 1. Read the table. Each line gives degrees north, then the two dates when the noon Sun is overhead there. 8: 10 April and 1 September. 10: 16 April and 27 August. 12: 22 April and 21 August. 13: 24 April and 18 August. 15: 1 May and 12 August. 17: 8 May and 5 August. 19: 15 May and 28 July. 20: 20 May and 24 July. 21: 25 May and 18 July. 22: 31 May and 12 July. 23: 10 June and 2 July. 2. Find the line nearest your city. 3. Circle the two dates on the calendar.
flow.say: The overhead Sun moves north from the equator in March. It reaches the Tropic of Cancer on 21 June and turns back. So it passes over each place once going north and once going south.
flow.kid: Find your city's line in the table. Read the two dates. Circle them on the calendar.
flow.parent: The dates can be a day out in some years. If your city is north of the Tropic of Cancer it has no zero shadow day. Then find the day when the noon shadow is shortest. It is 21 June.
flow.context: This is the table step of Zero Shadow Hunt. You read the two dates when the noon Sun is overhead in your city.

flow.do: 1. Draw a small upright stick on paper three times. 2. Under the first, draw its noon shadow in January. Under the second, on the first zero shadow day. Under the third, on 21 June. 3. Mark north and south on each drawing.
flow.say: In January the noon Sun is in the southern half of the sky, so the shadow points north. On a zero shadow day there is no shadow. Where is the noon Sun on 21 June, north or south of overhead? So which way does the shadow point?
flow.kid: Draw a stick three times. Draw its noon shadow in January, on zero shadow day, and on 21 June. Which way does June's shadow point?

ask.q: Which way does the noon shadow point in Chennai on 21 June?
good: South, because the Sun has gone north of overhead.
It is short, because the Sun is only about 10 degrees from overhead.

flow.parent: Between its two zero shadow days, a city has the noon Sun to its north, and noon shadows point south. In Chennai that is from about 24 April to 18 August. North of the Tropic of Cancer, noon shadows point north all year.
flow.context: This is the drawing step of Zero Shadow Hunt. You work out which way a noon shadow points before, on and after a zero shadow day.

flow.do: 1. Local noon is halfway between sunrise and sunset. Work it out from the times in a newspaper. 2. Extra, if sunlight reaches a floor in your home at noon: on your zero shadow day, stand a steel tumbler on the sunny floor at local noon and look for its shadow.
flow.say: Local noon is the middle of the day by the Sun, and it is usually not at twelve on the clock. Find the halfway point between today's sunrise and sunset.
flow.kid: Find the time halfway between sunrise and sunset. That is local noon. On zero shadow day, look for a tumbler's shadow then.
flow.think: People in Delhi never see a zero shadow day. What could they look for on 21 June that is nearly as good?
flow.parent: The extra step needs a grown-up, because it may mean going out on a terrace in strong sun. The shadow vanishes for only a few minutes. The whole activity works without it.
flow.context: This is the last step of Zero Shadow Hunt. You work out the time of local noon, so that you know exactly when to look on the day.

activities.title: My Own Season Wheel: how many seasons does your city really have?
activities.context: In this activity you make a season calendar for the place where you live, as the Noongar people and the old Tamil poets did for theirs. You decide how many seasons there are and what begins each one.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and a steel plate to draw round
a pencil, a ruler and colour pencils
an older relative or neighbour to ask, if you have one nearby

activities.record: Keep the wheel on a wall. Through the year, write the real date each time one of your seasons begins. Also keep a seasons journal: once in each season, on the same day, write one entry under five themes: plants, animals, weather, water and people.

setup.art: A large circle drawn on paper and divided lightly into twelve months round the rim.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a circle and mark the twelve months round its rim.

setup.art: The same wheel divided into five unequal coloured parts, each with a small drawing: a mango, a rain cloud, a kite, mist and a jasmine flower.
setup.caption: 2. Divide it into your own seasons. They need not be equal.

flow.do: 1. Draw round the plate. 2. Mark the twelve months round the rim, like the hours on a clock. 3. Together, list what changes through the year where you live. Think of rain, wind, heat, fruit in the market, flowers, birds, insects and festivals.
flow.say: Forget the seasons in schoolbooks for a moment. What really changes here through the year? What do you see, hear, smell and eat at different times?
flow.kid: Draw a circle. Mark the twelve months round it. List what changes where you live through the year.
flow.parent: Good clues are local ones: the first mangoes, jasmine or mallipoo prices, the kite winds of Aadi, mosquitoes, the smell of the first rain, foggy mornings, when the fan goes off at night.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Own Season Wheel. You list the changes that you can really notice in your own place.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many seasons the list needs. 2. Your child draws lines from the centre to divide the wheel. The parts need not be equal. 3. Give each season a name and one sign that begins it.
flow.say: How many seasons does our place have? Where does each one begin? A season can begin on a date. It can also begin when something happens, like the first rain.
flow.kid: Decide how many seasons your place has. Divide the wheel. Name each season. Choose a sign that starts it.

ask.q: Should your season begin on a fixed date, or when its sign appears? Why?
good: On a date, so that everyone can plan.
When the sign appears, because the rain does not read the calendar.
Either, with a reason.

flow.context: This is the deciding step of My Own Season Wheel. You choose the number of seasons, their names and what begins each one.

flow.do: 1. Colour each season and draw its sign. 2. Mark the two solstices and the two equinoxes on the rim. 3. Mark Pongal, Onam or the main festivals your family keeps.
flow.say: Now mark 21 June, 21 December, 20 March and 23 September on the rim. Do any of your seasons begin near them? Where do your festivals fall?
flow.kid: Colour your seasons. Mark the solstices and equinoxes on the rim. Mark your family's festivals.
flow.parent: There is no right answer. A child in Chennai may have a north-east rain season that a child in Jaipur lacks. A child in Shillong may want two rain seasons.
flow.context: This is the drawing step of My Own Season Wheel. You add the four marker days and your festivals, to compare the Sun's year with your own.

flow.do: 1. Show the wheel to an older relative or a neighbour, if you can. Ask whether the seasons have changed since they were young. 2. Compare your wheel with the six ritus.
flow.say: Compare your wheel with the six ritus: Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira. Which fit our place? Which do not? Who do you think the six were made for?
flow.kid: Show your wheel to an older person. Ask what has changed. Compare your seasons with the six ritus.
flow.think: If every town made its own season wheel, would India need one shared count as well? What for?
flow.context: This is the last step of My Own Season Wheel. You compare your own count with the old Indian count of six.

activities.title: The Wobbling Top: a fast spin and a slow circle
activities.context: In this activity you make a small top and watch its leaning axis trace a slow circle while it spins fast. The Earth's axis does the same over about 26,000 years, and that is why Pongal has slipped from the solstice.

materials.item: stiff card, such as a piece of a cardboard box
a steel tumbler to draw round
a short pencil, about 6 cm long, sharpened
scissors
a sketch pen
a smooth floor or a steel plate to spin on
a pambaram or any toy top, if you have one. Then skip step 1.

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the card and makes the hole. Keep the pencil point away from faces when the top is spinning.
activities.record: Write how many slow circles the axis made in 10 seconds, and whether the lean stayed the same. Draw the top with its two motions shown by two arrows.

setup.art: A cardboard circle with a short pencil pushed through its exact centre, point down, and a bright dot drawn near the rim.
setup.caption: 1. Push a short pencil through the centre of a card circle.

setup.art: The top spinning on a steel plate, leaning a little, with a dotted circle in the air showing the path of the pencil's upper end.
setup.caption: 2. Spin it and watch the top end of the pencil. It traces a slow circle.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up draws round the tumbler on the card and cuts out the circle. 2. Find the centre by balancing the circle on the pencil point. 3. A grown-up pushes the pencil through the centre, so that about 2 cm sticks out below. 4. Draw one bright dot near the rim.
flow.say: We are making a top. The pencil is its axis. The card must sit level and tight on the pencil.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut a card circle. Push a short pencil through the centre. Draw a dot near the rim.
flow.parent: If the card slips on the pencil, wind a rubber band round the pencil above and below the card. A lower card makes a steadier top.
flow.context: This is the making step of The Wobbling Top. A grown-up cuts a card circle and you fit a pencil through its centre as an axis.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess. 2. Spin the top between finger and thumb on the plate. 3. Watch the top end of the pencil.
flow.say: When the top slows and leans, what will its top end do? Will it stay leaning one way, fall straight over, or do something else? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what the leaning top will do. Then spin it. Watch the top end of the pencil.

ask.q: What did the top end of the pencil do?
good: It went round in a slow circle.
It kept its lean for a while, but the lean swung round.

flow.context: This is the guessing step of The Wobbling Top. You guess what a leaning, spinning top does, and then watch.

flow.do: 1. Spin the top again. 2. One person counts 10 seconds aloud. The other counts how many slow circles the top end of the pencil makes. 3. Try to count the spins of the dot in the same time. 4. Do this three times.
flow.say: The top has two motions. The fast one is the spin. The slow one is the wobble of its axis. Count the slow circles in ten seconds. Can you count the spins at all?
flow.kid: Spin the top. Count the slow circles of the pencil end in 10 seconds. Try to count the fast spins too.
flow.parent: Expect a few slow circles in 10 seconds and far too many spins to count. The wobble speeds up as the top slows down. If your top falls at once, push the card lower on the pencil.
flow.context: This is the counting step of The Wobbling Top. You compare the top's fast spin with the slow circling of its axis.

flow.do: 1. Give the Earth's numbers: one spin a day, and one slow circle of the axis in about 26,000 years. 2. Work out together how many spins the Earth makes in one circle of its axis. 3. Talk about what a slowly circling axis does to the stars behind the Sun on a given date.
flow.say: The Earth spins once a day. Its axis circles once in about 26,000 years. So where the axis points among the stars slowly changes. A calendar tied to the stars slips against the seasons, by about one day in 70 years.
flow.kid: The Earth spins once a day. The axis circles once in 26,000 years. How many spins is that?
flow.think: Pongal is now 24 days after the December solstice. If it slips one day in 70 years, how long ago did the two match?
flow.parent: 26,000 times 365 is about 9 and a half million spins. And 24 times 70 is 1,680 years, so the dates matched about 1,700 years ago. The top wobbles because gravity tries to tip it over. The Earth wobbles because the Moon and the Sun tug on the bulge round its middle.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Wobbling Top. You connect the top's slow wobble to the Earth's axis and to the date of Pongal.

activities.title: Summer on Mars, Winter on Uranus: try three other leans
activities.context: In this activity you reuse the ball and lamp from The Leaning Ball. You set the ball to the leans of Jupiter, Mars and Uranus, and count what kind of seasons each planet has.

materials.item: the dotted ball, the two tumblers and the lamp from The Leaning Ball
the four marked places round the lamp
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with a row for each planet: its lean, the lit dots on the northern ring at place 1 and at place 3, and one sentence about its seasons.

setup.art: Three balls on tumblers in a row: one standing almost upright, one leaning a quarter of the way over and one lying on its side with its top dot pointing sideways.
setup.caption: 1. Three leans: Jupiter almost upright, Mars like the Earth, Uranus on its side.

setup.art: The ball lying on its side on a tumbler with its top dot pointing straight at the lamp, and the whole upper ring in the light.
setup.caption: 2. For Uranus the top dot points at the lamp at place 1.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the three leans. Jupiter leans 3 degrees, which is almost upright. Mars leans 25 degrees, a little more than the Earth. Uranus leans 98 degrees, which is lying on its side. 2. Ask for a guess for each.
flow.say: Which planet will have the strongest seasons? Which will have almost none? What will a year feel like at the north pole of Uranus? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three planets, three leans. Which has the strongest seasons? Which has none? Guess. Say why.

ask.q: Which planet has the strongest seasons, and why do you think so?
good: Uranus, because it leans the most.
Any guess with a reason from The Leaning Ball.

flow.context: This is the guessing step of Summer on Mars, Winter on Uranus. You guess what seasons three other planets have from their leans.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Stand the ball almost upright for Jupiter. Count the lit dots on the northern ring at place 1 and at place 3. 3. Lean it a little more than a quarter of the way over for Mars. Count at place 1 and place 3.
flow.say: First Jupiter, then Mars. Keep the top leaning towards the lean wall at both places, as before.
flow.kid: Stand the ball almost upright. Count at place 1 and place 3. Then lean it like Mars. Count again.
flow.parent: Expect about 6 and 6 for Jupiter, and about 9 and 3 for Mars.
flow.context: This is the Jupiter and Mars step of Summer on Mars, Winter on Uranus. You count lit dots for an almost upright planet and for one leaning like the Earth.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ball on its side for Uranus, with the top dot pointing at the lean wall. At place 1 the top dot points straight at the lamp. 2. Count the lit dots on the northern ring at places 1, 2 and 3.
flow.say: Now Uranus. The top dot points at the lean wall, level with the floor. What happens to the northern ring at place one? And at place three?
flow.kid: Lay the ball on its side. Point the top dot at the lean wall. Count at places 1, 2 and 3.
flow.parent: Expect 12, about 6 and 0. At place 1 the whole northern ring is lit, so the Sun never sets there. At place 3 it never rises. A year on Uranus is 84 Earth years, so each of these lasts about 21 years.
flow.context: This is the Uranus step of Summer on Mars, Winter on Uranus. You count lit dots for a planet lying on its side.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the table. 2. Tell your child that Mars's path is more stretched than the Earth's, so on Mars distance matters too.
flow.say: On Mars, the path round the Sun is quite stretched. Mars gets much more sunlight when it is near the Sun. So Mars has seasons from its lean and from its distance. Is the rule 'distance does not matter' a rule for every planet?
flow.kid: Fill in your table. On Mars, distance matters too. Is 'lean, not distance' true for every planet?
flow.think: If you could choose a lean for a new planet, which would you choose for its living beings, and why?
flow.context: This is the last step of Summer on Mars, Winter on Uranus. You compare the three planets and test how far the Earth's rule reaches.

projects.title: The Noon Shadow Diary: six weeks of one stick (if sunlight reaches a floor in your home at noon)
projects.context: In this project you measure the noon shadow of one upright stick once a week for six weeks. The shadow shows the noon Sun climbing or sinking in the sky, which is the Earth's lean made visible.

materials.item: a place where sunlight falls on a flat floor at noon: a balcony, a terrace or the floor inside a window
a 1 litre plastic bottle filled with water, with its cap on
a straight pencil or straw and cello tape
a sheet of chart paper, and tape to fix it to the floor
a ruler and a pen
a newspaper or a calendar that gives sunrise and sunset times

projects.safety: Never look at the Sun. Look only at the shadow. A grown-up goes along if the sunny place is a terrace or an open balcony.

schedule.what: Make the shadow stick. Find the time of local noon. Mark the tip of the noon shadow and measure it. Guess what next week's shadow will do.
At local noon, mark and measure the shadow again.
At local noon, mark and measure the shadow again.
At local noon, mark and measure the shadow again.
At local noon, mark and measure the shadow again.
Mark and measure for the last time. Draw a line graph of the six lengths and explain it.

projects.record: Keep the chart paper with six dated marks. Keep a table with the date, the time of local noon, the shadow's length in centimetres and whether it points north or south. Draw a line graph of length against date.

setup.art: A plastic bottle full of water with a pencil taped upright against its side, the pencil tip level with a ruler mark at 20 cm.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a pencil upright to a full bottle, with its tip 20 cm above the floor.

setup.art: The bottle standing on chart paper in a patch of sunlight, with its outline drawn on the paper and a pen mark at the tip of the pencil's shadow.
setup.caption: 2. Draw round the bottle so it goes back in the same place. Mark the tip of the shadow at local noon.

setup.art: The same chart paper weeks later with six dated marks in a row, each a little further from the bottle outline.
setup.caption: 3. After six weeks you have six dated marks.

flow.do: 1. Tape the pencil upright to the side of the full bottle, with its tip exactly 20 cm above the floor. 2. Tape the chart paper to the sunny floor. Stand the bottle on it and draw round its base. 3. Work out local noon: the time halfway between today's sunrise and sunset. 4. At that time, mark the tip of the pencil's shadow and write the date. 5. Measure from the point under the pencil tip to the mark. 6. Ask for a guess about next week.
flow.say: This stick will show us how high the noon Sun is. A high Sun gives a short shadow. Will next week's noon shadow be longer, shorter or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tape a pencil to a full bottle. Stand it in the Sun at local noon. Mark the tip of the shadow. Guess next week's shadow.

ask.q: Will next week's noon shadow be longer or shorter, and why do you think so?
good: Shorter, because we are moving towards June and the Sun is climbing.
Longer, because we are moving towards December.
The same, if we are close to a solstice.

flow.parent: If the chart paper cannot stay on the floor, mark its corners on the floor with tape so that it goes back exactly. From 21 December to 21 June the noon Sun climbs, and from 21 June to 21 December it sinks. In Chennai and further south, the shadow can also swap from the north side to the south side.
flow.context: This is day 1 of The Noon Shadow Diary. You make a shadow stick, find local noon and mark the first shadow.

flow.do: On days 8, 15, 22 and 29: 1. Put the bottle back on its outline. 2. Work out local noon again, because it shifts by a few minutes. 3. Mark the tip of the shadow, write the date and measure the length.
flow.say: Before you measure, guess today's length from the last marks. Then check. Is the shadow changing by the same amount each week?
flow.kid: Put the bottle back on its outline. Guess today's shadow. Then mark it at local noon and measure it.
flow.wait: Come back once a week for four weeks.
flow.parent: Each visit takes about 8 minutes. If noon is cloudy, try the next day and write the true date. Near an equinox the shadow of a 20 cm stick changes by about 1 cm a week. Near a solstice it hardly changes at all.
flow.context: These are the four middle visits of The Noon Shadow Diary. Each week you mark and measure the noon shadow of the same stick.

flow.do: 1. On day 36, mark and measure the last shadow. 2. Draw a line graph of shadow length against date. 3. Your child writes what the graph shows and why.
flow.say: Look at your six marks. Which way did the noon Sun move, higher or lower? Did it move evenly? What will the marks do over the next six weeks?
flow.kid: Mark the last shadow. Draw a graph of your six lengths. Which way did the noon Sun move?
flow.think: The word solstice means 'the Sun stands still'. What would your marks look like in the weeks round a solstice?
flow.parent: If the marks hardly moved, you were near a solstice, and that is a good result. The stick did not move and the floor did not move. The change is the Earth's lean, seen from a new place on the orbit.
flow.context: This is the last day of The Noon Shadow Diary. You graph six weeks of shadows and say what they show about the Sun's height at noon.

games.title: Where on the Orbit? A clue card game
games.context: This is a clue card game with a small board of the Earth's orbit. Each card describes something happening on the Earth, and you must say where the Earth is on its path round the Sun.

printables.title: The board: the Sun, the orbit and 4 marker days
items: Draw the Sun as a small circle in the middle of a page.
Draw a big circle round the Sun for the Earth's orbit. Draw an arrow on it going anticlockwise.
Mark place J on the left of the circle. Write: 21 June.
Mark place S at the bottom. Write: 23 September.
Mark place D on the right. Write: 21 December.
Mark place M at the top. Write: 20 March.
The four stretches between the places are J to S, S to D, D to M and M to J.

printables.title: 20 clue cards: a clue on the front, the place and the reason on the back

items.f: It is the longest day of the year in Delhi.
items.b: Place J. On 21 June the northern end of the axis leans most towards the Sun.

items.f: It is the longest day of the year in Sydney.
items.b: Place D. On 21 December the southern end of the axis leans most towards the Sun.

items.f: Day and night are nearly equal everywhere, and India's days are growing longer.
items.b: Place M. After the March equinox the noon Sun moves north of the equator.

items.f: Day and night are nearly equal everywhere, and India's days are growing shorter.
items.b: Place S. After the September equinox the noon Sun moves south of the equator.

items.f: The noon Sun is overhead on the Tropic of Cancer, which crosses Gujarat and West Bengal.
items.b: Place J. This happens only on the June solstice.

items.f: The noon Sun is overhead on the Tropic of Capricorn.
items.b: Place D. This happens only on the December solstice.

items.f: The Earth is at its nearest to the Sun for the whole year.
items.b: Stretch D to M, just after D. Perihelion is in early January, in the northern winter.

items.f: The Earth is at its farthest from the Sun for the whole year.
items.b: Stretch J to S, just after J. Aphelion is in early July, in the northern summer.

items.f: Families in Tamil Nadu watch the Pongal pot boil over.
items.b: Stretch D to M. Pongal is about 14 January, 24 days after the December solstice.

items.f: Chennai has its first zero shadow day of the year.
items.b: Stretch M to J. About 24 April the noon Sun passes over Chennai on its way north.

items.f: Chennai has its second zero shadow day of the year.
items.b: Stretch J to S. About 18 August the noon Sun passes over Chennai on its way south.

items.f: At the North Pole the Sun has been up for three months, and will stay up for three more.
items.b: Place J. The Sun rises at the North Pole in March and sets in September.

items.f: At the North Pole the Sun rises after six months of night.
items.b: Place M. From the March equinox the North Pole leans into the light.

items.f: The south-west monsoon reaches Kerala.
items.b: Stretch M to J, just before J. The usual date is about 1 June.

items.f: The north-east monsoon is raining on Chennai.
items.b: Stretch S to D. It blows from October to December.

items.f: Kerala keeps Onam, as the heavy rains ease and the first rice is cut.
items.b: Stretch J to S, near S. Onam is in August or September.

items.f: It is Vishu in Kerala, Puthandu in Tamil Nadu and Baisakhi in Punjab.
items.b: Stretch M to J. These fall about 14 April, 25 days after the March equinox.

items.f: It is Nowruz, the new year of Iran and of the Parsis.
items.b: Place M. Nowruz is kept on the March equinox.

items.f: The noon shadow of a pole in Delhi is the longest of the year.
items.b: Place D. On 21 December the noon Sun is at its lowest in Delhi.

items.f: In Chennai, noon shadows point south.
items.b: Place J, and the stretches on either side of it, from about 24 April to 18 August. The noon Sun is then north of overhead.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Write each player's name at the top of a column.
Put one tally mark for each point.
Add up the marks when the pile is finished.

rules: Draw the board. Use a button or a coin as the Earth. Shuffle the 20 cards and put them clue side up in a pile.
Read the top card aloud. Do not turn it over.
The player whose turn it is puts the Earth on a place or on a stretch, and gives a reason. The reason must say which way the axis leans or where the noon Sun is.
Turn the card over. The right place or stretch earns 1 point. A reason that matches the back earns 1 more point.
Then the next player takes the next card. Take turns to go first.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Go through the whole pile. A score of 24 out of 40 is good, and 32 is very good. Then play again and try to beat your score.

setup.art: A hand-drawn board: a small Sun in the middle, a large circle with an anticlockwise arrow, and four marked places labelled J, S, D and M.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board with the four marker days.

setup.art: A pile of small cards beside the board, a button on the circle between D and M, and a child pointing at it.
setup.caption: 2. Read a clue. Put the button where the Earth must be.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board together, following the seven lines of the board printable. 2. Copy or cut out the 20 cards. 3. Put the button on J and ask which end of the axis leans towards the Sun there. Move it to S, D and M and ask again.
flow.say: The Earth goes round anticlockwise: June, September, December, March. At J the north leans to the Sun. At D the south does. Where is the Earth today?
flow.kid: Draw the board. Put the button on J. Which end leans to the Sun there? Now find today's place.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where on the Orbit. You draw the board of the Earth's path and find the four marker days on it.

flow.do: 1. Play the pile, following the rules. 2. After each card, the player gives the reason before the card is turned over. 3. Keep the score with tally marks.
flow.say: Read the clue. Put the Earth where it must be. Tell me why before we turn the card.
flow.kid: Read the clue. Put the Earth in its place. Say why. Then turn the card over.
flow.parent: The hardest cards are the nearest and farthest points, and the Chennai shadow card. If a reason is right but worded differently from the back, give the point.
flow.context: This is the playing step of Where on the Orbit. You place the Earth for each clue and give a reason before you check.

flow.do: 1. Add up the scores. 2. Each player picks the card that surprised them most and says why. 3. Together, make up one new clue card for your own city.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Now let us write a card of our own. What happens in our city at one point of the orbit?
flow.kid: Add up the points. Which card surprised you most? Make up a new card for your own city.
flow.think: Which clues would be different if this game were made by a child in Sydney?
flow.context: This is the last step of Where on the Orbit. You count the score and write one new clue card of your own.

games.title: Whose Season? A year-line card game
games.context: This is a card game about the many ways people divide the year. Each card names a season from one people's calendar. You say whose calendar it is from and place it on a line of the twelve months.

printables.title: The year line
items: Draw a long line across a sheet of paper turned sideways.
Divide it into 12 equal boxes and write the months, January to December.
Mark 20 March, 21 June, 23 September and 21 December with small Suns.

printables.title: 20 season cards: a season and a clue on the front, the calendar and the months on the back

items.f: Vasanta. Mango trees flower and the koel calls.
items.b: Sanskrit calendar of six ritus. Spring, about mid-March to mid-May.

items.f: Varsha. The clouds break and the rivers fill.
items.b: Sanskrit calendar of six ritus. The rains, about mid-July to mid-September.

items.f: Sharad. The rains end, the sky clears and the Moon is bright.
items.b: Sanskrit calendar of six ritus. Autumn, about mid-September to mid-November.

items.f: Shishira. Cool mornings with dew on the grass.
items.b: Sanskrit calendar of six ritus. Late winter, about mid-January to mid-March.

items.f: Kaar. Dark clouds gather and the first rains fall.
items.b: Old Tamil calendar of six seasons. The months of Aavani and Purattasi, about mid-August to mid-October.
