rules: Draw the year line. Shuffle the 20 cards and put them front side up in a pile.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Do not turn it over.
Say whose calendar the season comes from. Then lay the card on the year line, on a month when you think that season is on.
Turn the card over. The right calendar earns 1 point. A month that the back names earns 1 more point.
Leave the card on the line at its true place, so that the line fills up as you play.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? A score of 20 out of 40 is good on the first try. Play again and try to beat it.
Last round, for everyone together: look at the full line. Find two seasons from different peoples that fall at the same time. Say what each people was watching.

setup.art: A long strip of paper divided into twelve month boxes with four small Suns drawn at the solstices and equinoxes.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the year line with the twelve months.

setup.art: The year line with several small cards laid along it, and a child placing one more above the box for July.
setup.caption: 2. Lay each season card on the month where you think it belongs.

flow.do: 1. Draw the year line together. 2. Copy or cut out the 20 cards. 3. Tell your child the six calendars in the pile: Sanskrit, old Tamil, Noongar, ancient Egyptian, Chinese and the India Meteorological Department.
flow.say: People everywhere have divided the year, each in their own way. There are six calendars in this pile. Listen to each name and each clue. What were those people watching?
flow.kid: Draw the year line. Cut out the cards. There are six calendars in the pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whose Season. You draw a line of the twelve months and meet the six calendars in the game.

flow.do: 1. Play the pile, following the rules. 2. Before each card is turned, ask for the reason behind the month chosen. 3. Leave each card on the line at its true place.
flow.say: Whose season is this? Where on the year line does it go? Tell me what in the clue made you choose that month.
flow.kid: Read the card. Say whose calendar it is. Lay it on a month. Say why. Then turn it over.
flow.parent: Remember that Noongar country is in the Southern Hemisphere, so its hot season is in December. The clues are enough to place most cards within two months. The calendar is harder, and guessing it from the sound of the name is fair.
flow.context: This is the playing step of Whose Season. You place each season on the year line and give your reason before checking.

flow.do: 1. Add up the scores. 2. Play the last round together: find two seasons from different peoples that fall at the same time, and say what each people was watching. 3. Ask the closing question.
flow.say: Look at the whole line. Varsha, Kaar and Akhet all fall in the same months. One is named for rain, one for clouds and one for a flooding river. Which other pairs can you find?
flow.kid: Add up the points. Find two seasons from different peoples at the same time of year. What was each people watching?
flow.think: No two of these calendars cut the year in the same places. Is one of them more correct than the others?
flow.context: This is the last step of Whose Season. You compare seasons from different peoples that fall at the same time of year.

challenges.title: A Shade for the Window: block the May Sun, let in the January Sun
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. The noon Sun is high in summer and low in winter. You use that to design a ledge above a window, a chajja, that keeps the hot Sun out and lets the winter Sun in.
challenges.problem: A window in Delhi faces south and is 120 cm tall. From April to August the noon Sun is 73 degrees or more above the horizon. On 21 December it is only 38 degrees above the horizon. Design a ledge above the window that shades the whole window at noon from April to August. In December it must leave at least three-quarters of the window in sunlight. Build a model where 1 cm stands for 10 cm, and test it with a torch.
constraints: The window in the model is 12 cm tall and 8 cm wide.
The ledge is fixed. It may not be moved between summer and winter.
Test with the torch at 73 degrees and at 38 degrees above the table, held at least 50 cm away.
Use as little card for the ledge as you can.
materials: a shoebox or any cardboard box, and scissors
strips of card for the ledge, and cello tape
a torch, a ruler and a pencil
a protractor, to set the torch at 73 degrees and at 38 degrees
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the window in the box.
general: A flat ledge fixed along the top of the window. Indian builders call it a chajja.
A deeper ledge than needed, which is safe in summer but steals winter sunlight.
Upright fins at the two sides, which also block the low morning and evening Sun.
creative: A frame over the window with a creeper that is leafy in summer and bare in winter.
A row of thin slats tilted like the steps of a ladder, which pass low light and block high light.
A stone or wooden jaali, a screen cut with small holes, which breaks strong light into soft spots.
A pale shelf inside the window that bounces winter sunlight up onto the ceiling.
challenges.your_turn: Now design a shade for a window in your own home. Find out which way it faces. Remember that south of the Tropic of Cancer the noon Sun is in the north for part of the year. There is more than one good answer.

setup.art: A shoebox standing on its side with a window 12 cm tall cut in one face and a narrow card ledge taped along the top edge of the window.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a window 12 cm tall in the box. Tape a card ledge above it.

setup.art: A torch held high and far from the box, shining steeply down so that the ledge's shadow covers the whole window.
setup.caption: 2. Shine the torch from 73 degrees. The ledge should shade the whole window.

setup.art: The torch held lower, shining at a shallow angle so that light passes under the ledge and fills most of the window.
setup.caption: 3. Shine from 38 degrees. Most of the window should be lit.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a window 12 cm tall and 8 cm wide in one side of the box. 2. Stand the box so that the window is upright. 3. Read the problem and the constraints aloud.
flow.say: This box is a room in Delhi, and the window faces south. In May we want shade. In December we want the Sun to come in. One fixed ledge has to do both jobs.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut a window in the box. Stand the box upright. Read the problem.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Shade for the Window. A grown-up cuts a model window and you read what the ledge has to do.

flow.do: 1. Ask how deep the ledge should be, and why. 2. Your child draws the window from the side. A ray of light comes down at 73 degrees past the tip of the ledge. 3. Cut a first ledge of the guessed depth and tape it along the top of the window.
flow.say: How far must the ledge stick out to shade the whole window when the Sun is 73 degrees high? Draw it from the side first. Why do you think that depth will work?
flow.kid: Guess how deep the ledge must be. Draw the window from the side with a ray of light. Tape on your ledge.

ask.q: Why will your ledge keep out the high Sun but not the low Sun?
good: High light comes down steeply, so a small ledge throws a long shadow down the wall.
Low light slips in under the ledge.

flow.parent: A side drawing with a protractor gives a depth of about 3.7 cm. Let your child find it by drawing or by trying. The cutting needs a grown-up.
flow.context: This is the guessing step of A Shade for the Window. You guess the depth of the ledge and draw the light passing its tip.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim. 2. Hold the torch 50 cm from the window, 73 degrees above the table. Check with the protractor at the window. Is the whole window in shadow? 3. Hold the torch at 38 degrees. Measure how much of the window's height is lit. 4. Change the ledge and test again, until both rules are met with the least card.
flow.say: Test the summer Sun first, then the winter Sun. If summer light gets in, the ledge is too short. If winter light is blocked, the ledge is too deep. Change one thing and test again.
flow.kid: Shine the torch from 73 degrees. Is the window shaded? Now from 38 degrees. How much is lit? Change the ledge and try again.
flow.parent: A ledge about 3.7 cm deep just shades the 12 cm window at 73 degrees. At 38 degrees it shades only about 3 cm, so 9 cm, three-quarters, is lit. That is about 37 cm on the real window. A torch beam spreads, so hold it well back and aim the middle of the beam at the ledge. Trimming the ledge needs a grown-up.
flow.context: This is the testing step of A Shade for the Window. You test the ledge with a high torch and a low torch and improve it.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual solutions and the creative ones. 2. Your child chooses one to add or try. 3. Talk about a window in Chennai, where the June Sun is in the north.
flow.say: Builders in India have used chajjas and jaalis for hundreds of years. Which of these ideas would you add? Now think of Chennai. In June the noon Sun there is in the north. Which windows need a ledge?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Choose one to try. In Chennai the June Sun is in the north. Which windows need shade there?
flow.think: A tree outside a window is also a shade. What does a tree do that a ledge does not?
flow.context: This is the last step of A Shade for the Window. You compare your ledge with other solutions and think about a city further south.

challenges.title: A Calendar That Stays with the Seasons: design a leap rule
challenges.context: This is a design challenge with numbers. The year of the seasons is not a whole number of days. You design a rule for adding extra days, so that a calendar stays in step with the seasons for 1,000 years.
challenges.problem: The Earth takes 365.2422 days to go from one March equinox to the next. A calendar year must have a whole number of days. Design a rule that says which years get an extra day. After 1,000 years, the March equinox must still fall within one day of its date.
constraints: Every year has 365 or 366 whole days.
The rule must be simple enough to say in one or two sentences.
After 1,000 years the calendar may be wrong by at most one day.
Show the working for your rule.
materials: a calculator, if you have one
general: Add one day every 4 years. This is the Julian calendar of 46 BCE. Its year is 365.25 days, a little too long, so it slips about 8 days in 1,000 years.
Add one day every 4 years, but skip three of them in every 400 years. This is the Gregorian calendar of 1582, used across the world today. It slips about one-third of a day in 1,000 years.
The Indian national calendar of 1957 uses the same leap years as the Gregorian calendar, and starts its year on 22 March, just after the equinox.
creative: Add 8 extra days in every 33 years. This gives a year of 365.2424 days. It is linked to the calendar made in Persia in 1079 by a team that included the poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam.
Use no rule at all. Watch the sky and start the year on the day the equinox really happens. Iran's calendar today works this way.
Follow the Moon for months and add a whole extra month about every third year. Many Indian panchangams do this, and the extra month is called adhika masa.
challenges.your_turn: Now design a calendar for Mars. A Mars year is about 668.6 Mars days long. How many days will your ordinary year have, and which years get an extra day? There is more than one good answer.

setup.art: A notebook page with the number 365.2422 written large and a child's working below it.
setup.caption: 1. Start from the true length of the year: 365.2422 days.

setup.art: A long strip of paper marked off in years, with every fourth box coloured and a few of the coloured boxes crossed out.
setup.caption: 2. Decide which years get an extra day, and test your rule over 1,000 years.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. First test a calendar with no extra days at all. Each year it falls short by 0.2422 of a day. 3. Your child works out how far it slips in 100 years.
flow.say: Suppose every year had exactly 365 days. Each year the calendar would finish about a quarter of a day too soon. How far would it slip in 100 years? What would that do to the date of the mango season?
flow.kid: A year is 365.2422 days. A calendar has 365. How many days does it slip in 100 years?
flow.parent: 0.2422 times 100 is about 24 days. In 100 years the seasons would come more than three weeks late by the calendar.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Calendar That Stays with the Seasons. You find out how fast a calendar with no leap days slips.

flow.do: 1. Test the rule 'one extra day every 4 years'. 2. Work out the average length of its year. 3. Take away the true year and multiply by 1,000.
flow.say: Now add one day every four years. What is the average length of the year? Is it too long or too short? How far does it slip in 1,000 years?
flow.kid: Add a day every 4 years. What is the average year now? How far does it slip in 1,000 years?

ask.q: Is the 4-year rule too long or too short, and by how much in 1,000 years?
good: Too long. The average year is 365.25 days.

flow.context: This is the testing step of A Calendar That Stays with the Seasons. You test the rule of one leap day every four years.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs a better rule. 2. They work out its average year and its slip in 1,000 years. 3. They say the rule aloud in one or two sentences.
flow.say: The four-year rule adds about eight days too many in 1,000 years. How could you take some back, or add them in a different pattern? Design a rule and test it.
flow.kid: The 4-year rule adds 8 days too many in 1,000 years. Design a better rule. Test it. Say it in two sentences.
flow.parent: One good path: 1,000 years need about 242 extra days, and the 4-year rule gives 250. So drop about 8 leap days in 1,000 years, for example every year that divides by 125. Accept any rule that is within one day and shows its working.
flow.context: This is the designing step of A Calendar That Stays with the Seasons. You invent your own leap rule and test it over 1,000 years.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual and creative solutions aloud. 2. Compare each with your child's rule. 3. Read the Mars problem and start on it.
flow.say: People have solved this in Rome, in Persia and in India, in different ways. Which is closest to yours? Which would you rather live by: a rule, or watching the sky?
flow.kid: Read how other people solved it. Which is closest to your rule? Then try a calendar for Mars.
flow.think: A calendar that follows a rule can be printed years ahead. A calendar that follows the sky is never wrong. Which matters more to you?
flow.context: This is the last step of A Calendar That Stays with the Seasons. You compare your rule with real calendars and begin one for Mars.

worksheets.title: Lean, light and the four marker days

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: The Earth spinning on its axis
The Earth's journey round the Sun
The noon Sun is furthest north or south
The noon Sun is over the equator
The Earth's nearest point to the Sun
items.why: Rotation gives the day and revolution gives the year. The tilt, carried round the orbit, gives the solstices and the equinoxes.

items.p: One rotation of the Earth takes about ____ hours.
items.why: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours. That spin gives day and night.

items.p: The Earth is nearest to the Sun in June.
items.why: False. The Earth is nearest in early January and farthest in early July. So nearness does not give India its summer.

items.p: A torch shines on a card. The card leans back. What happens to the patch of light?
opts: It moves but keeps its size
items.why: The same light is spread over a longer patch, so each square gets less. If you chose 'the same', try it once more with a torch and a book.

items.p: Put these in order through one year, starting from 20 March.
items.why: The Earth passes the four marker days in this order, about three months apart.

items.p: 21 June or 21 December? Sort each line.
items: Noon Sun over the Tropic of Cancer
Noon Sun over the Tropic of Capricorn
Sun up all night at the North Pole
items.why: On 21 June the northern end of the axis leans towards the Sun. On 21 December the southern end does.

items.p: The Sun rises at 6:00 and sets at 6:40 in the evening. How many minutes of daylight is that?
items.why: From 6:00 to 6:00 in the evening is 12 hours, which is 720 minutes. Add 40 minutes to get 760.

items.p: Where does the length of the day change least through the year?
items.why: Kanyakumari is nearest the equator, where every day is close to 12 hours. The change grows as you go north.

items.p: Draw the Sun and the Earth on 21 June. Show the axis, the equator and which half has summer.
items.a: The axis leans with its northern end towards the Sun. The half of the Earth facing the Sun is lit. The northern half is labelled summer and the southern half winter.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lean clearly and keeps the Earth about the same distance from the Sun as in any other month.
items.art: A blank box with a small Sun at the left and space for the Earth at the right.

items.p: A friend says, 'Summer is when the Earth is close to the Sun.' Give two facts that do not fit this idea.
items.a: The Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, in India's winter. Australia has summer when India has winter, at the same distance from the Sun. A torch moved 1 cm in 30 hardly changes its patch.
items.why: A strong answer gives two facts the distance idea cannot explain. The best are the January date and the opposite seasons of the two hemispheres.

items.p: The wind that brings rain to Kerala about 1 June is the south-west ____.
items.why: A monsoon is a wind that changes direction with the seasons. The south-west monsoon blows from the sea from June to September.

items.p: The hottest weeks of the year always fall exactly on the longest day.
items.why: False. The ground and the sea take weeks to warm up, so the hottest weeks usually come later. In much of India they come in May, before the monsoon clouds arrive.

items.p: Match each season name to the people who use it.
items.why: Each people divided the year by what mattered on their own land: rain, dew, cold storms, a flooding river and the time to sow.

items.p: About when is Pongal, counted from the December solstice?
items.why: Pongal is about 14 January, 24 days after the solstice of about 21 December. About 1,700 years ago the two fell on the same day.

items.p: Why must the axis keep pointing the same way for the two hemispheres to swap seasons?
items.a: If the axis always leaned towards the Sun, the north would always have summer. Because it keeps pointing one way in space, the north leans towards the Sun on one side of the orbit and away from it on the other side.
items.why: A strong answer says that the lean stays fixed while the Earth moves to the other side of the Sun.

worksheets.title: Shadows, day lengths and season counts

items.p: A ring has 9 lit dots out of 12. Each dot is 2 hours. How many hours of daylight?
items.why: 9 times 2 is 18 hours. The other 3 dots are 6 hours of night.

items.p: A card leans until the torch patch is twice as long. How much light does each square get now?
items.why: The same light covers twice the area, so each square gets half. If you chose 'the same', remember that the torch did not get brighter.

items.p: On an equinox, a place at the equator has the noon Sun overhead.
items.why: True. On the two equinoxes the noon Sun is overhead at the equator, so that is a zero shadow day there.

items.p: Chennai has two zero shadow days each year, about 24 April and 18 ____.
items.why: The overhead Sun passes Chennai once on its way north in April and once on its way south in August.

items.p: Does this city have a zero shadow day? Sort each one.
items.why: Only places between the two tropics ever have the Sun overhead. Delhi, Lucknow and Srinagar are north of the Tropic of Cancer.

items.p: Sort these journal notes into the five themes: plants, animals, weather, water and people.
items: the mango trees are in flower
a cool wind comes after the hot dry spell
the family gathers for a cousin's wedding
items.why: Each note tells you about one theme only. A flowering tree is about plants, a calling bird is about animals, and a cool wind is about weather.

items.p: In June the noon shadow of a pole in Chennai points south. Explain why.
items.a: On 21 June the noon Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, about 23 and a half degrees north. Chennai is at 13 degrees north. So the Sun is about 10 degrees to the north of overhead, and the shadow falls to the south.
items.why: A strong answer compares the place of the overhead Sun with the place of Chennai.

items.p: Put these cities in order, from the smallest change in day length to the largest.
items.why: The change grows with distance from the equator: under 1 hour, about 1 and a half hours, about 3 and a half hours and about 4 and a half hours.

items.p: Why is Delhi's coldest week in January and not on 21 December?
opts: The Earth is farthest from the Sun in January
The ground keeps losing heat for some weeks
January days are shorter than December days
The Sun gives less light in January
items.why: After the shortest day, the ground still loses more heat each night than it gains each day, for a few more weeks. The Earth is in fact nearest the Sun in January.

items.p: Draw a year wheel with the six ritus. Mark where the two solstices fall on it.
items.a: Six equal parts in order: Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta, Shishira. The June solstice falls in Grishma and the December solstice in Hemanta.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the ritus in the right order and shows that each is about two months long.
items.art: A blank circle with twelve small month marks round its rim.

items.p: When does summer begin?

views.says: Summer begins on the June solstice, when the Sun is highest. That is a real event in the sky that anyone can measure.
Summer is the hottest stretch of the year. In India that is March to May, before the rains. The solstice comes too late.

views.who: A person using the old Chinese or Irish calendar
views.says: The solstice is the middle of summer. Summer is the season of the strongest light, so it begins in early May.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what the other two are watching.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The astronomer watches the Sun's height. The weather officer watches the heat. The old calendars watch the light.
items.why: No view is marked right. Each is a true account of a different thing, and seasons can be counted by any of them.

items.p: Match each festival to its place in the Sun's year.
pairs: About 24 days after the December solstice
About 25 days after the March equinox
August or September, as the heavy rains ease
items.why: Some festivals are fixed to the season and some to the stars. Those fixed to the stars now fall about three and a half weeks after the solstice or equinox they once marked.

items.p: Sankranti slips about 1 day later every 70 years. How many days does it slip in 700 years?
items.why: 700 divided by 70 is 10. So in 700 years it moves about 10 days later.

items.p: Mars leans about 25 degrees and Jupiter about 3 degrees. Which has stronger seasons? Explain why.
items.a: Mars. A lean of 25 degrees gives each half of Mars a time of steep light and long days, then slanting light and short days. Jupiter is almost upright, so every place gets nearly the same light all year.
items.why: A strong answer links the size of the lean to how much the slant of light and the day length change.

items.p: In the monsoon months the wind over India blows from the same direction as in winter.
items.why: False. A monsoon is a wind that turns round with the seasons. In summer it blows from the south-west sea. In winter it blows from the north-east.

items.p: Three of these are caused by the Earth's lean. Which one is not?
opts: Longer days in June in Delhi
items.why: Day and night come from the Earth's rotation. They would happen even on an upright Earth. The other three need the lean.

items.p: The Sun is 147 million km away in January and 152 million in July. What is the difference, in million km?
items.why: 152 minus 147 is 5 million km. That is only about 3 parts in every 100 of the distance.

items.p: Delhi is at about 29 degrees north. How far from overhead is its noon Sun on 21 December?
items.why: The Sun is then overhead 23 and a half degrees south of the equator. Add Delhi's 29 degrees north to get about 52 degrees.

items.p: Explain why Chennai's winter is milder than Delhi's. Use what you know about slant.
items.a: In Chennai the noon Sun is at most about 37 degrees from overhead, so the ground still gets about 8 parts in 10 of the straight-on light. In Delhi it is about 52 degrees, so the ground gets only about 6 parts in 10. Delhi's days are also shorter in December.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two slants and the two day lengths. A full answer may add that Chennai is beside a warm sea.

items.p: On Mars, distance from the Sun matters for the seasons as well as lean.
items.why: True. Mars has a much more stretched orbit than the Earth. It gets about 45 parts in 100 more sunlight at its nearest than at its farthest.

items.p: The slow wobble of the Earth's axis, once in about 26,000 years, is called ____.
items.why: Precession slowly changes which stars lie behind the Sun on a given date. It is why star-based calendars slip against the seasons.

items.p: A calendar year is 0.0078 of a day too long. How many whole days does it slip in 1,000 years?
items.why: 0.0078 times 1,000 is 7.8, which rounds to 8 days.

items.p: Should Makar Sankranti be moved back to the December solstice?

views.says: No. Sankranti is the day the Sun enters Makara. That is what the word means, and families have kept it this way for about 2,000 years.

views.who: An astronomer on Meghnad Saha's committee
views.says: Yes. The festival was made to mark the Sun turning north. That now happens three weeks earlier. A calendar should tell the truth about the seasons.
Pongal is for the harvest. My rice is ready in mid-January. For me the date is already right.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The first keeps the tie to the stars. The second keeps the tie to the solstice. The third keeps the tie to the crop.
items.why: No view is marked right. This is a real argument in India, and each side protects something that the festival means.

items.p: Rotation, revolution or tilt? Sort what each one mainly gives us.
items: The stars circling the Pole Star each night
items.why: The spin gives the day. The journey gives the year. The lean, carried along on the journey, gives the seasons.

items.p: Design a test to show that an upright Earth has no seasons. What would you change and count?
items.a: Carry a dotted ball round a lamp, first leaning and then upright. Keep the lamp, the ball and the distance the same. Count the lit dots on a ring at four places. Leaning gives different counts. Upright gives the same count everywhere.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the lean, keeps everything else the same and names something to count.

items.p: Sulochana Gadgil described the monsoon as what?
opts: A rain belt that follows the overhead Sun
Wind made by the Earth's spin
Rain sent down by the Himalaya
items.why: She showed that India's monsoon behaves like the band of rain clouds near the equator, moved north in summer. The sea breeze idea is Edmond Halley's, from 1686.

items.p: Put these planets in order, from the smallest lean to the largest.
items.why: Jupiter leans about 3 degrees, the Earth about 23 and a half, Mars about 25 and Uranus about 98.

items.p: Draw a pole's noon shadow in Chennai on 21 June and on 21 December. Mark north and south.
items.a: On 21 June the Sun is a little north of overhead, and a short shadow points south. On 21 December the Sun is well to the south, and a longer shadow points north.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both the swap of direction and the difference in length.
items.art: Two blank boxes side by side, each with a small upright pole on a ground line and the letters N and S at the ends.

items.p: Your city needs its own season calendar. Name three seasons you would give it, and the sign that begins each.
items.a: Any three seasons that fit the child's place, each with a sign that can be noticed. For example: the mango heat, which begins when the first mangoes reach the market.
items.why: There is no single answer. A strong answer uses signs from the child's own place and not from a book.

items.p: Day and night are exactly 12 hours each on the day of the equinox.
items.why: False, though it is close. The air bends sunlight and the Sun is a wide disc, so the day is about 12 hours and 7 minutes. Day and night are truly equal a few days before the March equinox.

items.p: The half of the year when the noon Sun moves north is called ____.
items.why: Uttarayana runs from the December solstice to the June solstice. Dakshinayana is the other half, when the noon Sun moves south.

quiz.p: Which motion of the Earth gives us the year?
quiz.why: One revolution round the Sun is one year. Rotation gives the day. If you chose rotation, think of a top that spins while it slides round a table.

quiz.p: About how long does the Earth take to go once round the Sun?
quiz.why: The extra 6 hours add up to one day in four years, which is why we have leap years.

quiz.p: In which month is the Earth nearest to the Sun?
quiz.why: Early January. This is winter in the north, so nearness cannot be the cause of summer.

quiz.p: Why does slanting sunlight warm the ground less than light from overhead?
opts: It comes from a cooler part of the Sun
It is spread over more ground
quiz.why: The same light covers a larger patch, so each square metre gets less. It also crosses more air on the way.

quiz.p: It is winter in Srinagar. What season is it in Sydney, Australia?
quiz.why: When the northern end of the axis leans away from the Sun, the southern end leans towards it. If you chose winter, picture the leaning ball at place 3.

quiz.p: What would happen to the seasons if the Earth's axis stood upright?
quiz.why: With no lean, every place would get the same slant of light and 12 hours of day all year.

quiz.p: On which day is the noon Sun overhead on the Tropic of Cancer?
quiz.why: On the June solstice the northern end of the axis leans most towards the Sun.

quiz.p: What is true on the two equinoxes?
opts: The Earth is nearest the Sun
Day and night are nearly equal everywhere
The Sun does not rise in India
quiz.why: On an equinox the line between day and night passes through both poles, so every place gets about 12 hours of each.

quiz.p: Which city has the biggest difference between its longest and shortest day?
quiz.why: Srinagar is furthest from the equator. Its longest day is about 4 and a half hours longer than its shortest.

quiz.p: The Sun stays up for about six months at the North Pole. Why is the pole still very cold?
opts: Its rays arrive at a slant and spread thin over the ground
The pole is the farthest place from the Sun
The Sun's day is short there
quiz.why: The Sun does rise there in spring, and it stays up all summer. But it stays low in the sky, so its light spreads over a wide patch of ground. The pole is not the farthest place from the Sun, and the Sun's day is long there, not short.

opts: A wind that reverses with the seasons
quiz.why: The word means season. The wind blows from the south-west sea in summer and from the north-east in winter.

quiz.p: The old Tamil calendar and the Sanskrit calendar both count how many seasons?
quiz.why: Both count six, with different names and starting points. India's weather office counts four.

quiz.p: Why does Pongal now come about three weeks after the December solstice?
opts: The axis slowly wobbles, shifting the stars
The calendar lost three weeks in 1957
quiz.why: Pongal follows the stars. Precession slowly shifts the stars behind the Sun, about one day in 70 years.

quiz.p: A seasons journal has five themes: plants, animals, weather, water and people. Which theme does this entry fit? 'The tap ran dry in April and is running again in July.'
quiz.why: That note is about water in the tap. A note about heat or wind would go under weather, and a note about who came to the house would go under people.

applications: Builders set the depth of a chajja, the ledge above a window, from the height of the noon Sun in summer and in winter.
Solar panels in India are tilted towards the south by about as many degrees as the place is north of the equator, so that they face the Sun squarely over the year.
Farmers choose sowing dates by the monsoon and by day length. Many rice varieties flower only when the days shorten.
Calendar makers add leap days, or a whole extra month, to keep festivals and seasons together.
The India Meteorological Department forecasts the date the monsoon will reach Kerala, and the whole country plans by it.
Astronomers use the yearly shift of nearby stars, caused by the Earth's revolution, to measure how far away the stars are.
Scientists who study planets round other stars ask about each planet's lean, to judge what its seasons may be like.

maths.problem: In Lean or Distance, the upright patch is 6 cm long. At 52 degrees it is 9.6 cm long. What fraction of the straight-on light does each square now get?
maths.explain: 6 divided by 9.6 is 0.625, which is five-eighths. The same light is spread over a longer patch.
maths.context: In Lean or Distance you compare the length of each leaning patch with the upright patch.
maths.why_maths: Dividing turns two lengths into a share, which you can compare between cities.

maths.problem: The Earth is 147 million km from the Sun in January and 152 million km in July. About what percent further is it in July?
maths.explain: The difference is 5 million km. 5 divided by 147 is about 0.034, which is about 3 percent.
maths.context: The Earth's distance from the Sun changes a little through the year.
maths.why_maths: A percent shows how small the change is beside the whole distance.

maths.problem: In Chennai on 21 June the Sun rises at 5:43 and sets at 6:37 in the evening. How long is the day?
maths.explain: From 5:43 to noon is 6 hours 17 minutes. From noon to 6:37 is 6 hours 37 minutes. Together they make 12 hours 54 minutes.
maths.context: In Four Cities, Two Days you turn sunrise and sunset times into day lengths.
maths.why_maths: Working out a duration lets you compare days in different cities and months.

maths.problem: Delhi is 29 degrees north. On 21 June the noon Sun is overhead at 23 and a half degrees north. How many degrees from overhead is the noon Sun in Delhi?
maths.explain: 29 minus 23 and a half is 5 and a half. In December you add the two numbers and get 52 and a half degrees.
maths.context: The slant of the noon Sun depends on how far a place is from the spot where the Sun is overhead.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting two angles gives the slant of sunlight for any city on any marker day.

maths.problem: A year of the seasons is 365.2422 days. How many extra days must a 365-day calendar add in 400 years, to the nearest whole day?
maths.explain: 0.2422 times 400 is 96.88, which rounds to 97. The Gregorian calendar adds exactly 97 leap days in 400 years.
maths.context: A calendar needs leap days to stay with the seasons.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small decimal by many years shows how a tiny yearly gap grows.

maths.problem: Makar Sankranti is 24 days after the December solstice. It slips about 1 day every 70 years. About how many years ago did the two match?
maths.explain: 24 times 70 is 1,680. So the two matched about 1,700 years ago.
maths.context: A calendar tied to the stars slowly slips against the seasons.
maths.why_maths: A steady rate lets you work backwards to a date nobody alive has seen.

maths.problem: In The Leaning Ball, the northern ring had 9, 6, 3 and 6 lit dots at the four places. What is the average number of lit dots over the year?
maths.explain: 9 plus 6 plus 3 plus 6 is 24. 24 divided by 4 is 6. Over a whole year, every place gets about half its time in daylight.
maths.context: In The Leaning Ball you count lit dots at four places round the lamp.
maths.why_maths: An average shows what stays the same when the seasons change.

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. Lean or Distance (core) needs a torch, a tube, a card and a dark room. The edge of a torch patch is soft, so each patch is measured twice and the family's own upright length is used for every sum. Expected lengths for a 6 cm patch are 6.0, 6.1, 7.5 and 9.7 cm at 5, 10, 37 and 52 degrees, and about 2 mm of growth for the 1 cm move. A family that sees no change at all in the distance test has a true result. The Leaning Ball (core) needs a ball, three rubber bands and a lamp level with the ball. The usual slip is turning the ball to face the lamp. Counts within one dot of 9, 6, 3 and 6 are good. Four Cities, Two Days uses Sun times worked out for 21 June and 21 December and rounded to the minute. They can differ by a minute or two from a newspaper. The True Shape of the Year needs only a plate and a ruler. Zero Shadow Hunt works on paper, and its sunny step is extra. The zero shadow dates can be a day out in some years. The Wobbling Top needs a grown-up to cut the card. A card top spins for 10 to 20 seconds, which is enough to see the slow circle. The Noon Shadow Diary needs sunlight on a floor at noon once a week and is outside the core. Near a solstice its marks hardly move, and the steps say so. A Shade for the Window needs a grown-up to cut the box. The torch must be held well back, because its beam spreads. Both games are written out in full with 20 cards each, and each can be played alone. Nothing needs a garden or an animal, and nobody looks at the Sun in any step. Facts were checked on 26 November 2026: the distances and dates of nearest and farthest, the lean, the solstice and equinox dates, the day lengths, the zero shadow dates, the monsoon dates, the Calendar Reform Committee, Hipparchus and Timocharis, the planets' leans, and the three sets of authors on the monsoon and on the Moon. The story is made up. The three Roots teachings are paraphrased, not quoted. The season months for ancient Egypt and for the Noongar calendar are approximate. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel but not watched.
